## Abstract Objectives: Since its founding in 1989, the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine (SAEM) has accepted thousands of abstracts for presentation at its annual meeting. We reviewed abstracts to characterize temporal changes in study design, abstract topics, quality scores, and proportion of abstracts published as manuscripts. 

Methods: In this serial cross-sectional study, we compiled accepted SAEM abstracts at 5-year intervals (1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020) and then randomly se-lected 100 abstracts from each year for review by two investigators. We documented each abstract 's study design, sample size, and whether it was a single-center or mul-ticenter study. We assigned each abstract to the most appropriate topic category. Applying SAEM's abstract scoring system from 2020, we calculated the mean overall quality score per year. Finally, we searched PubMed to determine if abstracts from 1990–2015 meetings were published as manuscripts. 

Results: The number of accepted abstracts increased from 180 in 1990 to 879 in 2020 ( +388%). The most common study design changed from laboratory study in 1990 (22%) to cohort study in 2020 (44%; p < 0.001). The median study sample size increased over time, from 105 (interquartile range [IQR] 25–389) in 1990 to 544 (IQR 102–2067) in 2020 ( p < 0.001). Multicenter studies have become more com-mon (19% in 1990 vs. 40% in 2020; p = 0.001). The most common topic categories also changed from cardiology/pulmonary/airway (40%) and orthopedic/trauma/burn (17%) in 1990 to health services research/health policy/operations (25%) and cardi-ology/pulmonary/airway (22%) in 2020. There was a 20% increase in overall quality scores ( p < 0.001). Between 37% and 49% of the abstracts reviewed from each year were later published as manuscripts, with no significant change over time ( p = 0.33). 

Conclusions: Over the past 30 years, there have been significant changes to the study designs, topics, and quality scores of SAEM meeting abstracts. However, conversion of abstracts to published manuscripts remains a challenge. 1222 | Ս CHANGES IN SAEM ABSTRACTS, 1990 ҃ 2020 

## I NTRO D U C TI O N 

Scientific abstracts are frequently presented at the major meetings of professional and academic societies. Importantly, these presen-tations facilitate the dissemination of new research, often prior to the publication of a scientific manuscript based on that same data. 1In emergency medicine (EM), one of the major meetings at which abstracts are presented is the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine (SAEM) Annual Meeting. 2Briefly, SAEM was formed in 1989 via the merger of the University Association for Emergency Medicine (UAEM) and the Society of Teachers of Emergency Medicine (STEM). 3 This merger was undertaken in recognition of the overlap between research and education and, accordingly, SAEM has always focused on furthering both research and education. Research abstracts are selected for presentation at every SAEM Annual Meeting. 2 As part of the selection process, SAEM initially used a simple 4-item scale for abstract scoring, which was replaced by a more detailed approach in 1998; another iteration, which was made publicly available, was launched in 2015. 4 The evolving scoring system has provided a more objective approach for judging abstract quality and also educated EM researchers on essential aspects of high-quality research. Although SAEM has included scientific abstract presentations as part of its annual meeting since its founding, it is unclear if the characteristics of these abstracts have changed over time. We aimed to characterize temporal changes in the study design, abstract top-ics, quality scores, and the proportion of meeting abstracts subse-quently published as manuscripts. 

## M E TH O DS Study design 

In this retrospective study, we reviewed a random sample of ab-stracts from among all of those accepted to the SAEM Annual Meeting between 1990 and 2020. The Mass General Brigham Human Research Committee reviewed this study and classified it as exempt. This report adheres to the STROBE guidelines. 5

## Data collection 

We compiled accepted SAEM abstracts at 5-year intervals, from 1990 to 2020 (i.e., for 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020). We then randomly selected 100 abstracts from each cho-sen year for review using = RAND(), the random number feature of Microsoft Excel. Briefly, we assigned a random number between 0 and 1 to every accepted abstract and then sorted these random numbers from lowest to highest; the reviewed abstracts were those with the lowest 100 numbers in each year. We chose 100 ab-stracts per year because this would provide sufficiently narrow 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for key characteristics to allow meaningful comparisons across years. Each abstract was reviewed by at least two trained research assistants (VPD, HHI). When there were any discrepancies ( <10%), one of the authors (KMB) reviewed the two items to resolve the discrepancy. To keep KMB blinded to the year when reviewing dis-crepant scores, abstract text was copied over from the source PDFs to a separate document without identifying information; individual abstracts could be identified by searching for the abstract number or title. Additional methods and results describing agreement between trained research assistants and one investigator are available as sup-plemental materials accompanying the online article (Table S1). 

## Measurements 

For each abstract, we documented the following information: study type (basic, clinical, population [Methods S1]), study design (labora-tory, case report, case series, cross-sectional, case–control, cohort, randomized controlled trial, meta-analysis, qualitative, other), study sample size, and whether the study was a single-center or multi-center study. We also created a list of 18 abstract topic categories from those provided by SAEM over the 30-year period and assigned each ab-stract to the most appropriate category: abdominal/gastrointesti-nal/genitourinary, cardiology/pulmonary/airway, education/ethics/ faculty, geriatrics/palliative, infectious diseases, international EM, health services research (HSR)/health policy/operations, neurology, obstetrics/gynecology, orthopedic/trauma/burn, pediatrics, emer-gency medical services (EMS)/disaster/wilderness, psychiatry/social EM, public health, research methods, technology/simulation, toxi-cology/pharmacology, and other diseases (Methods S2). Using the latest (2020) version of SAEM's scoring system, 6 we also scored all abstracts on a scale of 0–2 based on seven criteria: clarity of objectives, choice of approach, validity, statistics, scope, importance of topic, and publication readiness. The maximum score (highest quality) is 14 points. Finally, we documented whether there was a corresponding publication in PubMed for abstracts accepted 1990–2015; thus, even the 2015 abstracts had 5 years to achieve manuscript publication. We documented that a publication was directly from the abstract if the content of the manuscript was substantially the same as that of the abstract, even if the title and authors of the manuscript varied slightly from the original SAEM Annual Meeting abstract (Methods S3). Additional methods describ-ing measurements are available as supplemental materials accompa-nying the online article. 

## Data analysis 

Data analysis included descriptive statistics, presented as propor-tions or as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs). We conducted unadjusted analyses using chi-square tests, Fisher's exact test, and Ս | 1223 CAMARGO ET AL Kruskal-Wallis tests, as appropriate, to assess the association be-tween abstract characteristics and abstract year. Analyses were done using Stata 15.1 (StataCorp). A two-tailed p < 0.05 was consid-ered statistically significant. We did not adjust for multiple testing so statistically significant results should be interpreted with caution. 

## R E S U LT S 

Overall, the number of abstracts accepted to the SAEM Annual Meeting increased from 180 in 1990 to 879 in 2020 ( +388%). Of the 7 years reviewed (e.g., 1990, 1995, and so forth), the year with the highest number of abstracts accepted was 2015 (1037; Figure 1). 

## Study type and design 

The proportion of studies that were clinical remained consistent throughout the study period (64% in 1990 vs. 63% in 2020); by con-trast, the proportion of basic science studies decreased (20% vs. 2%), and the proportion of population health studies increased (16% vs. 35%; Table 1). Over the study period, the most common study design changed from laboratory study in 1990 (22%) to cohort study in 2020 (44%, p < 0.001). Notably, only 1% of abstracts in 2015 and 2020 were laboratory studies. Twenty percent of abstracts in 1990 and 1995 were cohort studies—this proportion rose to 34% in 2000 and remained at least 34% for all subsequent years. Case– control studies decreased over time, from 14% in 1990 to 4% in 2020 (Figure 2, Figures S1 and S2). 

## Study sample sizes 

The median sample size increased over time, from 105 (IQR 25–389) in 1990 to 544 (IQR 102–2067) in 2020 ( p < 0.001). There were some intervals where the median sample size increased dramati-cally. Specifically, between 1990 and 1995, the median sample size increased from 105 (IQR 25–389) to 199 (IQR 52–592). Between 2015 and 2020, it increased from 295 (IQR 100–1370) to 544 (IQR 102–2067). Multicenter studies became more common over time (19% of studies in 1990 vs. 40% in 2020, p = 0.001; Table 1, Figure S2). 

## Abstract topic categories 

In 1990, the most common topic categories were cardiology/pulmo-nary/airway (40%), orthopedic/trauma/burn (17%), EMS/disaster/ wilderness (16%), and toxicology/pharmacology (14%). In 2020, the most common topic categories were HSR/health policy/operations (25%), cardiology/pulmonary/airway (22%), technology/simulation (18%), and education/ethics/faculty (15%). Looking across the 30-year study period, cardiology/pulmonary/airway remained the most common topic category from 1990 until 2005. From 2010 through 2020, HSR/health policy/operations was the most common topic category. Cardiology/pulmonary/airway has remained the second most common topic category during these more recent years. Other topics that significantly increased between 1990 and 2020 included technology/simulation (2% vs. 18%, respectively), psychiatry/social EM (0% vs. 11%), education/ethics/faculty (6% vs. 15%), and infec-tious diseases (5% vs. 12%, all p < 0.05). Other topics that signifi-cantly decreased between 1990 and 2020 included EMS/disaster/ wilderness (16% vs. 3%) and toxicology/pharmacology (14% vs. 7%, both p = 0.01; Table 1). 

## Abstract quality scores 

Overall quality scores increased from a median of 10 (IQR 8–11) in 1990 to 12 (IQR 10.5–13) in 2020. Scores increased among the following categories between 1990 and 2020: clarity of objec-tives, choice of approach, statistics, scope, and publication readi-ness (all p < 0.01). Scores for validity ( p = 0.08) and importance of topic ( p = 0.42) did not significantly change between 1990 and 2020 (Table 2). ## D I S CU S S I O N 

From 1990 to 2020, there was a clear increase in the number of scientific abstracts accepted for presentation at the SAEM Annual Meeting. Moreover, there were important changes in the most com-mon study designs, increases in both sample size and the proportion of studies that were multicenter, and changes in most common topic categories. There was also an increase in overall abstract quality scores, although not in every scoring category. There was also no significant change in the proportion of abstracts subsequently pub-lished as manuscripts. To our knowledge, this is the first study to as-sess the change in characteristics of abstracts accepted to the SAEM Annual Meeting over the three decades since the Society's founding. Our results are similar to those found in a 1999 study by Singer and colleagues. 7 Briefly, they reviewed UAEM abstracts from 1974 and 1983, then SAEM abstracts from 1989 and 1997. They noted changes in abstract characteristics and quality even in the early years after SAEM's founding. For example, they found an increase in the proportion of studies with power calculations and tests of signif-icance, which would likely mean an increase in “statistics” score and overall quality score, as we found. They similarly found an increase in study sample size during the early years of SAEM (25 [IQR 24–182] in 1989 vs. 129 [IQR 46–416] in 1997). We also found similar results to Porturas and Taylor, 8 who inves-tigated abstracts of EM articles from 1980 to 2019 within six highly cited journals. Although our topic groupings were not identical, Porturas and Taylor found a decrease in research involving cardiac arrest over the study period, while we found a decrease in abstracts focused on cardiology/pulmonary/airway. Similar to our results, Porturas and Taylor also found a large decrease in the proportion of abstracts classified as basic science. On the other hand, Porturas and Taylor found only a modest increase (0.6%) in the proportion of abstracts classified as mental health and substance abuse research, while we found an 11% increase in abstracts classified as psychia-try/social EM over the study period. The inclusion of social EM in our topic category may account for part of this. Further, there was a relatively high number of psychiatry/social EM abstracts in 2020, which was after the study period used in the Porturas and Taylor publication. One area that requires improvement is the proportion of meeting abstracts that are later published as full manuscripts. Although there probably is no one “right” answer, we estimate that that at least 80% of abstracts should proceed to manuscript publication. We found that approximately one-third to one-half were later published as manuscripts over the study period. Other studies similarly found that less than half of SAEM abstracts were published as manuscripts. For example, Callaham and colleagues 9 found that 41% of SAEM abstracts in 1991 were published as manuscripts, similar to the 46% we found to be published from the 1990 meeting. Li and colleagues reviewed all SAEM abstracts from 1997 and from 1999–2001. They found that between 35% and 40% were published as manuscripts per year. 10 Among abstracts accepted in 2000, they found that 38% were published manuscripts (compared to the 40% we found pub-lished in our sample from 2000). 10 They found that 19% to 24% were published within 1 year (compared to our 1990–2015 review, which found 21%–24% published within 1 year), 12%–17% 1 year later (compared to 8%–17%), and 10%–11% 2 years later (compared to 2%–11%). 10 Likewise, Gottlieb and colleagues 11 reviewed abstracts accepted to multiple EM conferences, including SAEM, from 2011 to 2015. They found that 49% of SAEM abstracts from during this time were later published as manuscripts. This was the same propor-tion of abstracts that we identified as published manuscripts in 2010 (49%) but higher than the proportion in 2015 (37%). In related work, Clemency and colleagues 12 examined EMS ab-stracts and publication following abstract presentation at multi-ple meetings, including SAEM, and found that 53% EMS abstracts from SAEM were later published. Adhikari and colleagues 13 exam-ined publication rates of ultrasound, EMS, and toxicology abstracts submitted to both SAEM and ACEP from 1998 to 2008. Publication rates were low (23%, 23%, and 21%, respectively), suggesting little difference by topic. The publication rate for SAEM abstracts since 1990 is middling compared to those of abstracts accepted to non-EM meetings. For example, publication rates of SAEM abstracts were lower than those accepted to: the Dutch Surgical Society meetings (69%), 14 American Society of Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology (56%), 15 Orthopedic Society of North America (53%), 16 Skeletal Society of Radiology (51%), 17 and the American Heart Association (50%). 18 Publication rates of SAEM abstracts were similar to those of abstracts accepted to the American College of Cardiology (43%), the European Society of Cardiology (38%), 18 and the North American Menopause Society (38%). 19 On the other hand, publication rates of SAEM abstracts were higher than those abstracts accepted to the American Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (25%) 20 and two wound conferences (12%). 21 Even the highest proportions suggest ample room for improvement. 

## LI M ITATI O N S 

Given the subjective nature of some of the data collection (e.g., the SAEM scoring system), it is possible that a different set of reviewers would have documented different results for these items. However, our approach was aligned with SAEM's actual scoring system, where each abstract is assigned to multiple reviewers. Furthermore, any discrepancies, between both the subjective and the objective items, were further reviewed for reconciliation. While it is possible that information bias was introduced (e.g., data abstracters were aware of the year of each abstract), the investigator who resolved scor-ing discrepancies in the SAEM scoring was blinded to the abstract Ս | 1227 CAMARGO ET AL year. Another possible limitation relates to the need to collapse topic categories given the substantial changes in potential abstract top-ics from 1990 to 2020, but these decisions were made with input of multiple experienced researchers, and these arguably more “gen-eral” categories still convey a clear change in common topic cate-gories over time. Finally, we note that many of the characteristics overlap (e.g., multicenter studies generally will have larger sample sizes) but we did not perform multivariable analyses to address this relatedness. Our goal was to describe what happened over the past 30 years and the observed trends are true regardless of which fac-tor stands out in a stratified or multivariable model. We speculate that increases in collaborative research and in the availability of large administrative datasets underlie some of the observed results. We also speculate that widespread adoption of the SAEM abstract scor-ing criteria has led to significant improvements in the quality of the accepted research. 

## CO N C LU S I O N S 

Research presented at the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine Annual Meeting has changed significantly over the past 30 years. Overall, studies have become larger and are now more likely to be multicenter, and the most common topics have changed over time. Further, the scientific quality of abstracts has improved, reflected by an increase in scores over time. One area for improve-ment is the subsequent publication of accepted abstracts as full manuscripts. We look forward to witnessing (and participating) in the continued evolution of research presented at the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine Annual Meeting, as this research will remain a key component of emergency medicine research dis-semination worldwide.

## Abstract Objectives: This systematic review identified and assessed psychometric properties of the available screening tools to identify patients with unmet palliative care (PC) needs in the emergency department (ED). 

Methods: A comprehensive search of electronic databases and the gray literature was conducted. Two independent reviewers completed study screening and inclu-sion, data extraction, and quality assessment. A descriptive summary of the results was reported using median of medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs). 

Results: A total of 35 studies were included, involving the assessment of 14 unique screening tools. The most commonly used screening tool was the surprise question (SQ; n = 12 studies), followed by the Palliative Care and Rapid Emergency Screening (P-CaRES) tool ( n = 8), and the screening for palliative and end-of-life care needs in the emergency department (SPEED) instrument ( n = 4). Twelve of the included studies re-ported on the psychometric properties of the screening tools, of which eight of these studies assessed the performance of the SQ to predict patient mortality. Overall, the median sensitivity (63%, IQR 38%–78%) and specificity (75%, IQR 57%–84%) of the SQ to predict mortality at 1 or 12 months was moderate. While the median posi-tive predictive value of the SQ was low (32%, IQR 16%–40%), the median negative predictive value was high (91%, IQR 88%–95%). Across the studies, the proportion of patients identified as having unmet PC based on the criteria of the screening tools ranged from 5% to 83%. 

Conclusions: This review identified 14 unique screening tools used to identify adult patients with unmet PC needs in the ED. One screening tool, the SQ, was found to have moderate sensitivity and specificity to accurately predict future patient mortal-ity. Additional research is needed to better understand the clinical value of this and the other available tools prior to their widespread implementation.

## I NTRO D U C TI O N 

With the increase in emergency department (ED) visits among patients with advanced or end-of-life (EOL) conditions, 1,2 early integration of palliative care (PC) services into the ED has been recommended by initiatives like the Choosing Wisely Campaign. 3 For many patients, the ED offers a unique opportunity to initiate these connections; how-ever, identifying patients with unmet PC needs and finding the time to initiate discussions in a chaotic, fast-paced environment such as the ED can be challenging. As such, several screening instruments/tools have been developed for the purpose of assisting emergency physi-cians and other health care providers to identify patients with unmet PC needs , including the surprise question (SQ) 4 and the Palliative Care and Rapid Emergency Screening (P-CaRES) tool. 5,6 Despite the availability of multiple screening tools to identify patients with unmet PC needs in the ED, the performance of these tools has not been well established making the recommendation for one particular tool over the others difficult. 7 With the publication of various new studies, this systematic review conducted an updated assessment of the available screening tools to identify ED patients with unmet PC needs in the ED. 

## M E TH O DS Protocol 

A study protocol was developed and registered on PROSPERO (regis-tration #CRD42018086178) to define the objectives, selection criteria, data collection, and analysis. This review followed the recommenda-tions of the PRISMA guidelines for reporting of systematic reviews. 8

## Inclusion/exclusion 

Studies assessing the ability of a screening tool to identify adult pa-tients with unmet PC needs in the ED were eligible for inclusion in this review. To be eligible studies had to apply the screening tool on adult patients presenting to the ED. Studies did not need to utilize a control group or reference standard nor to report on the psycho-metric properties of the screening tools to be included in the review. While prospective and retrospective studies were eligible for inclu-sion, reviews, editorials, or case studies were excluded. 

## Outcome 

The primary outcome of interest pertained to the performance of the screening tools, including psychometric properties such as sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive values (PPV), negative predictive values (NPV), and/or likelihood ratios (LRs). Secondary outcomes of interest included metrics on the reliability and validity of the tools, proportion of patients with unmet PC needs, referrals to PC consultations or hospice services, disposition of index visit (e.g., discharge or hospitalizations), mortality (either within the ED or fol-lowing ED discharge), and subsequent health care utilization (e.g., hospitalization, ED visits). 

## Search methods for identification of studies 

A search was conducted by an experienced health research librar-ian (S.C.) on the following databases: OVID Medline, Ovid EMBASE, OVID Health and Psychosocial Instruments, EBSCO-CINAHL, SCOPUS, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, Cochrane Library, and PROSPERO using controlled vocabulary and key words representing the concepts “emergency department” and “palliative care” and “screening.” Searches were adjusted appropriately for dif-ferent databases. Searches were last updated in August 2021. No publication or language limits were applied. Results were exported to RefWorks citation management system. Detailed search strate-gies are available in Appendix 1. A search of the gray literature consisted of a search of Google Scholar, clinical trial registries (e.g., clinicaltrials.gov, Cochrane Central Register of controlled trials, and controlled-trials.com), backward and forward SCOPUS searches of included studies, bib-liographies from known reviews, and abstracts from emergency medicine conferences including Canadian Association of Emergency Physicians (2015–2021), Society for Academic Emergency Medicine (2015–2021), and the American College of Emergency Physician Abstracts (2015–2021). 

## Selection of studies 

The title and abstract of studies identified in the literature search were screened for eligibility by two independent reviewers (M.G.C., M.K., E.H.Y., or S.W.K.). The full text of studies identified as poten-tially eligible were retrieved and reviewed for inclusion based on predefined inclusion criteria by two independent reviewers (M.G.C., M.K., E.H.Y., or S.W.K.). Disagreements were resolved via consensus. 

## Data extraction 

Two independent reviewers (M.G.C., M.K., E.H.Y., or S.W.K.) ex-tracted predefined outcomes onto standardized electronic forms. Disagreements were resolved via discussion. If a study reported outcomes such as mortality over multiple time points, only the last time point was considered in the meta-analysis. 

## Quality assessment 

For studies reporting the psychometric properties of the screen-ing tools, the methodologic quality was assessed using the Quality Ս | 1231 KIRKLAND ET AL .Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS) 9 and Standards for Reporting Diagnostic accuracy studies (STARD) 10 tools. The quality of observational cohort studies that did not assess the psychometric properties was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). 11 Quality assessment was conducted by in-dependent author reviewers and disagreements were resolved via consensus. Two authors (E.H.Y., S.W.K.) reviewed 34 of the 35 stud-ies, and the one study 12 for which S.W.K. was the lead author was instead reviewed by E.H.Y. and J.M. 

## Data synthesis 

A descriptive summary of the results was reported. Summary tables were created to report on the study characteristics, screening tools, psychometric properties, and other outcomes. Medians and inter-quartile ranges (IQRs) were calculated, and a median of medians ap-proach was taken for reporting the “average” effect. No sensitivity or subgroup analyses were conducted. While some studies reported outcomes based on ED visits or presentations, 12,13 for the purposes of this review, the unit of analysis was based on individual patient data. If available, performance of screening tools was assessed based on the positive ( +) or negative ( ƴ) LRs, with +/ƴ LRs ~0.5 to 2 rated as unhelpful (poor performance), mid-range (5 < + LR < 10; 0.5 < ƴLR > 0.1) rated as moderate performance, and the extremes (+LR > 10; ƴLR < 0.1) rated as excellent performance. 14 

## R E S U LT S Search results 

Once duplicates were removed, a total of 5491 title and abstracts were screened following database and gray literature searches (see Figure 1). A total of 5237 studies were found to be irrelevant and ex-cluded from the study, resulting in the full-text review of 254 stud-ies. The full texts of 219 studies were excluded for various reasons (see Figure 1), resulting in the inclusion of 35 studies in the review. 

## Study characteristics 

The majority of studies were conducted in the United States (see Table 1). Twelve of the included studies were conference abstracts. 15-26 The majority of studies reported screening unmet PC needs in ED patients with specific EOL conditions or patients re-quiring admission (see Table 1). 12,13,15-21,24- 42 Across the 35 included studies, a total of 14 unique screening tools were assessed (see Table 1 and Appendix 2). The majority of studies did not utilize an-other screening tool as a reference standard, except for three studies that used screening tools that had been previously used to identify unmet PC needs in patients in other clinical settings. 37,43,44 Other studies utilized medical or death records as a reference standard for the assessment of the accuracy of the screening tool to predict patient mortality. 4,19,27-29,41,42,44,45 One study 42 and one conference abstract 18 were found to utilize a similar database of patients. Both studies reported different objectives and outcomes, except for one overlapping outcome (proportion of patients with unmet PC needs). To reduce the risk of duplicate data, only the proportion of patients with unmet PC needs as reported in the published study 42 was in-cluded in the analysis. 

## Screening tool characteristics 

## SQ The most commonly assessed screening tool was the SQ (see Table 1). While most of the included studies applied the original SQ (Would you be surprised if the patient died in the next 12months?), 4,16,19,28,44,45 some studies utilized a modified SQ (Would you be surprised if the patient died in the next 30days?). 15,17,18,27,29,42 A negative response (e.g., the physician would not be surprised if the patient died during a given time frame) was suggestive that the patient had unmet PC needs. Assessment of unmet PC needs was reported to have been completed by the attending emergency physicians in all but two of the included studies (see Table 1). 16,44 A small number of studies applied the SQ to patients with a specific clinical condition including heart failure, 45 advanced cancer, 28 chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), 29 and sepsis, 17 while the majority of studies applied the SQ to patients without a specific clinical condition. 4,15,16,18,19,27,44 Some studies fur-ther specified that they strictly applied the SQ to patients who were to be admitted to hospital, 15,17,18,27,29,42 admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), 19 or to any patients older than 65 4 or 70years. 44 P-CaRES tool Eight studies 12,13,20,21,30,31,32,33 utilized the P-CaRES tool, which con-sists of a list of potential EOL conditions including advanced demen-tia or central nervous system disease, cancer, COPD, chronic renal failure, end-stage liver disease, septic shock in patients over 65 years old, and other conditions with a high chance of accelerated death. 5If the patient presented with at least one EOL condition, the asses-sors completed the second domain, selecting risk factors for unmet PC needs from a checklist that included previous ED visits or hospi-talizations in the past 6 months, uncontrolled symptoms, functional decline, uncertainty about goals of care and/or caregiver distress, and a negative response to the SQ. 5 Based on the criteria of the P-CaRES tool, patients were identified as having unmet PC needs if they presented with at least one EOL condition and two or more risk factors for unmet PC needs. Some studies modified either the checklist of EOL conditions listed on the screening tool 12 or the list of risk factors for unmet PC needs (see Appendix 2). 32 Three studies strictly applied the P-CaRES tool on older or geriatric patients. 13,30,33 For the majority of studies, emergency physicians completed the 1232 | Ս

## Primary outcome 

## Performance Twelve of the 35 included studies reported the psychometric properties of the PC screening tools. From these 12 studies, vari-ous psychometric properties of the SQ were reported in nine of the studies, 4,15,19,27-29,42,44,45 with the performance of the P- CaRES tool, 13 the SST, 37 and A-qCPR 41 being assessed in three different studies. None of the included studies reported the psychometric properties of the SPEED tool or the other screening tools identi-fied in this review. Of the nine studies assessing the SQ, eight assessed its ability to predict patient mortality at 30 days 27,29,42 or 12 months 4,19,28,44,45 respectively using either official death re-cords or the patients' medical charts as the reference standard (see Table 2 , Figure 2). The overall median sensitivity of the SQ to predict mortality was 63% (IQR 38%–78%), while the median spec-ificity was 75% (IQR 57%–84%). The overall median PPV of the SQ was 32% (IQR 16%–40%) while the median NPV was 91% (IQR 88%–95%). The sensitivity of the SQ to predict patient mortality at 30 days was lower (range 12%– 43%) 27,29,42 than at 12 months (range 57%–89%; 4,19,28,44,45 see Figure 2). Similarly, the specificity of the SQ was higher among studies assessing patient mortality at 30 days (range 82%–95%) 27,29,42 than at 12 months (range 40%– 79%). 4,19,28,44,45 One study reported that the SQ had a +LR of 2.68 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.68–10.64) and a ƴLR of 0.92 (95% CI 0.76–1.11) for predicting 30-day mortality, 29 while another study reported a +LR of 2.5 (95% CI: 1.7, 3.7) and a ҽLR of 0.56 (95% CI: 0.4, 0.8) for predicting 12 month mortality. 44 One study reported that the modified-SQ had poor predictive properties for mortality at 6 and 12 months (see Table 2). 42 One study reported that the SQ had poor predictive properties for admission from the ED, prolonged length of stay (LOS), frailty, and readmission to hos-pital (see Table 3), 44 while another study reported that the SQ had low sensitivity (35%), high specificity (89%), and high NPV (97%) when used to predict the use of PC resources. 15 Psychometric properties of three other screening tools were reported. ## Secondary outcomes 

## Reliability/validity One study reported that the 13-item SPEED instrument had strong concurrent validity with domains of the Needs at the End-of-life Screening tool (NEST), with a Cronbach coefficient alpha of the SPEED instrument ranging from 0.716 to 0.991. 43 Following a corrected item correlation, the Cronbach coefficient of the SPEED instrument ranged from 0.326 to 0.970. 43 Another study reported that the SQ had moderate to strong correlation with the Caregiver Burden Score and Risk Instrument for Screening in the Community, but a poor correlation between the Clinical Frailty scale and the EQ-5D. 44 While Tineo et al. 40 did not assess the psy-chometric properties of their screening tool, their study reported that an unpublished pilot study found that their screening tool had acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach coefficient = 0.699). Patients with unmet PC needs The proportion of patients identified as having unmet PC needs var-ied among studies evaluating different screening tools and even among the studies assessing the same instruments (see Figure 3 and Table 3). Based on the criteria of the SQ, the median propor-tion of patients found to have unmet PC needs was 31% (IQR 15%–49%), 4,15,17,19,27-29,42,44,45 while the median proportion of patients identified as having unmet PC needs using the P-CaRES and SPEED instrument was 32% (IQR 30%–55%) 12,13,20,21,30-33 and 62% (IQR 52%– 72%), 21,22,23,43 respectively. The range of patients identified with the other palliative screening tools ranged considerably from 12% to 80% (median 36%, IQR 25%–71%; see Figure 3 and Table 3). 24,26,34,36,37,40,41 PC consultations Eighteen studies reported on PC consultations among patients with unmet PC needs; however, outcome reporting varied considerably (see Table 3). Two studies reported on the proportion of patients with unmet PC needs who had received an ED-based PC consulta-tion, which ranged from 1.4% 12 to 12%. 27 The proportion of patients with unmet PC needs who were hospitalized and received a PC con-sultation was reported to be 8%, 24 13%, 15 47%, 29 and 55% 19 across four studies. Patients with unmet PC needs who received a PC con-sultation postdischarge was reported to be 5%, 28 6%, 31 11%, 37,38 and 29% 12 in five studies. ## D I S CU S S I O N 

With an increase in ED visits among patients with EOL conditions, there is a need to identify those with unmet PC needs. While a previous systematic review published in 2016 included seven stud-ies assessing different screening tools or interventions, 7 the cur-rent systematic review conducted a comprehensive and updated search of the literature and identified 35 studies utilizing 14 unique

Despite the increase in published studies, the performance of the majority of screening tools remain infrequently reported, limiting the ability to make any clear recommendations for their widespread implementation. Of the screening tools assessed across the included studies, the psychometric properties of the SQ were the most commonly reported. The SQ exhibited moderate ability to predict mortality; however, per-formed better at predicting long-term mortality (within 12 months) than short-term mortality (within 30 days), while offering limited assistance to clinicians. For example, assuming a pretest probability of unmet PC needs in the populations at baseline of approximately 30%, given these results, the LRs are insufficient to confidently rule in a case when positive (30% increased to 45%) and insufficient to confidently rule out a case when negative (30% decreased to 18%) with certainty. Overall, strictly using the SQ to identify patients with unmet PC needs will result in referral of a large number of patients to PC services who may not benefit from them. Considering the costs and limited availability of PC services in the ED/hospital, screening tools with excellent performance are recommended to ensure the ap-propriate use of limited resources and improved quality of care. The results of our review are similar to those of another sys-tematic review that assessed the performance of the SQ across various clinical settings (e.g., ED, inpatient ward, ICU, general practice clinics, cancer centers). 47 That review reported that the SQ performed poorly to moderately as a predictive tool for death (sensitivity 67%, 95% CI 55.7%–76.7%; specificity 80.2%, 95% CI 73.3%–85.6%; +LR 3.4, 95% CI 2.8–4.1; ƴLR 0.41, 95% CI 0.32– 0.54) and that the SQ performed worse among patients with non-cancer conditions. 47 Unfortunately, the current review was unable to provide further clarity due to a limited reporting across the in-cluded ED studies. For example, the majority of studies assessing the SQ enrolled patients with various medical conditions; how-ever, these studies did not specify how the SQ performed among any subgroup of patients with advanced conditions. In addition, the majority of included studies utilized emergency physicians as the assessors of the SQ, and so it is unclear whether the perfor-mance of the SQ varies among user groups (e.g., emergency physi-cians, nurses, or other specialists) or whether prior training in PC impacts performance. Further assessment into factors (e.g., spe-cific EOL conditions, assessors, setting/context where this screen-ing tool is applied) that could influence the performance of the SQ to predict mortality appear warranted. The other most commonly assessed screening tools were the SPEED instrument 22,23,43,46 and the P- CaRES tool. 12,13,20,21,30-33 While one study found that the SPEED instrument had high re-liability compared to similar survey questions from previous val-idated tools, 43 the accuracy of SPEED is unclear. The original 11-item SPEED instrument was subsequently shortened to include 5 items to allow the tool to be more readily integrated into the patient 's bedside assessment 46 ; however, the psychometric prop-erties of the modified 5-item SPEED instrument have not been reported. The P- CaRES tool was found to have excellent content validity 5 and to have excellent accuracy in correctly recommend-ing PC consults when used by emergency physicians in various written case vignettes. 6 In the current review, the accuracy of the P- CaRES tool when applied to adult ED patients was infrequently reported, with only one study comparing the ability of trained chaplains to use the P- CaRES tool to identify ED patients with unmet PC needs compared to emergency physicians. 13 While the evidence suggests that the SPEED 43 and P- CaRES 5,6 tools have excellent content reliability/validity, additional studies assessing their accuracy in identifying unmet PC needs in ED patients are needed. For the other screening tools identified in this review, there is insufficient evidence to recommend any one over the SQ, P- CaRES, or SPEED tools for identifying unmet PC needs in the ED. One study found that the SST tool had high sensitivity and specificity to identify patients with unmet PC needs 37 ; how-ever, additional studies are needed. Importantly, given the poor to moderate performance of the SQ, additional studies assessing and reporting the performance characteristics of other available screening tools such as P- CaRES and SPEED are necessary. The proportion of patients identified as having unmet PC needs varied considerably across the included studies, even among stud-ies using the same screening tools, which could be the result of many factors. First, the patient population that was screened for unmet PC needs varied, with some studies screening only patients 65 years or older, 4,44 while other studies specifically screened pa-tients who were admitted to hospital or the ICU 18,19,27 or any pa-tients with specific clinical conditions 29,45 or specifically patients with established EOL conditions. 28,30,35 As previously mentioned, the performance of the SQ to predict mortality appears to decrease among patients with non–cancer-related conditions, 47 and at this point, it is unclear whether other patient demographic or clinical characteristics impacted the performance of the other PC screen-ing tools. Second, it was unclear how the screening tools were im-plemented within the ED, including when and how the screening tool was completed, whether health care staff were trained in the use of the screening tool, and time needed to complete the screen-ing process. It is possible that differences in how the screening tools were implemented could have impacted the performance of the tools across the studies. Finally, the variation in the proportion of

patients identified with unmet PC needs by the screening tools may be related to the inconsistent criteria for unmet PC needs across the tools. For example, some screening tools such as the P-CaRES and SPEED tools incorporated combinations of factors including fre-quent ED/hospitalizations, lack of family support or GOC planning, and uncontrolled symptoms in identifying whether or not patients were considered to have unmet PC needs. Other tools, such as the SQ, strictly used the expected likelihood of death in a prespecified period of time as their sole indicator of unmet PC needs, without considering any other physical, psychological, or socio-related factors. Given the complexity of the concept of unmet PC needs among patients with EOL conditions, it may be difficult to establish simple and quick screening tools such as the SQ to effectively and accurately identify patients in need of PC services. While the proportion of patients with unmet PC needs identified across the studies varied, the summary estimates do provide some useful information; for example, the median proportion of patients with unmet PC needs ranged between 32% and 35% and could be used in future study planning. In addition, the proportion of patients with unmet PC needs who received a PC consult either in the ED or in hospital varied among the studies yet tended to be low. It is pos-sible that some studies may have been conducted in EDs/hospitals that provide additional PC services compared to other studies, which could explain some of the variation in PC consultation referrals among the studies. It is unclear, however, whether screening for unmet PC needs prompted emergency physicians to more likely request PC consultations across some of the included studies, despite no explicit intervention to promote PC interventions. Various factors have been found to impact PC consultation rates including patient race and age, 48 and research has also suggested that inpatients with noncancer EOL conditions were more likely to undergo delays in receiving refer-rals to in-hospital PC consultations. 49 Finally, the available evidence suggests that approximately two of every three patients with unmet PC needs are hospitalized and that patients with unmet PC needs are likely to make subsequent ED visits. Further research assessing the demographics and clinical characteristics/ED management of pa-tients identified as having unmet PC needs could help physicians and providers understand their health care needs. 12,50 

## LI M ITATI O N S 

There are some limitations of the methods employed in this re-view to consider. While the risk of publication bias exists, multiple steps were taken to attenuate these risks, including an extensive search of the literature and no limitations based on language, pub-lication status, or year of publication. Moreover, steps were taken to reduce the risk of selection bias including the utilization of two independent reviewers to identify eligible studies to minimize the risk of missing any available studies. In addition, there were some inconsistencies identified by the STARD and QUADAS quality as-sessment tools with respect to the reporting of performance in-cluding blinding, test reproducibility, and assessors training. The methodologic quality of the majority of studies that did not assess psychometric properties was low primarily due to a lack of a com-parative group and inconsistent outcome and follow-up reporting. Moreover, there was a lack of a clear “reference standard” for the identification of patients with PC needs across the studies. The ma-jority of studies assessing the accuracy of the SQ to predict mortal-ity utilized death certificates or medical records as their reference standard to confirm patient death. Otherwise, a handful of studies utilized screening tools used other clinical settings to identify pa-tients with unmet PC needs 37,43,44 ; however, it is unclear how effec-tive these “reference standards” are in identifying ED patients with unmet PC needs. Finally, few comparative studies were performed, making selection of a preferred tool(s) for practice difficult. This review was unable to assess the ease in which any of these tools could be implemented into ED practice due to a limited report-ing of fidelity/implementation strategies across the included studies. While information related to training and time needed to administer the screening tools was not reported across the studies, it is likely that the low complexity of the SQ, which required a single yes or no response from attending physicians, makes it an appealing screening tool to utilize in a busy environment such as the ED and is perhaps one reason why it was the most commonly investigated. Given the fast-paced environment of the ED, screening tools that have high accuracy, but are complex or cumbersome to apply, will likely not gain widespread acceptance. 

## CO N C LU S I O N S 

This review identified 14 unique screening tools used to identify ED patients with unmet PC needs; however, the clinical utility of the majority of these tools to identify patients who would benefit from timely PC services remains unclear due to limited reporting on their performance. The SQ was found to have moderate predic-tive ability for long-term mortality; nonetheless, given the state of the evidence, there is insufficient evidence to recommend one particular screening tool for widespread use in the ED setting to accurately identify patients with unmet PC needs. While additional research assessing the performance and utility of these tools is recommended, before doing so health care providers and admin-istrators should assess the context in which screening tools have been tested and identify those they believe might be of clinical value in their unique settings.

## Abstract 

Pragmatic clinical trials (PCTs) focus on correlation between treatment and outcomes in real-world clinical practice, yet a guide highlighting key study considerations and design types for emergency medicine investigators pursuing this important study type is not available. Investigators conducting emergency department (ED)-based PCTs face multiple decisions within the planning phase to ensure robust and mean-ingful study findings. The PRagmatic Explanatory Continuum Indicator Summary 2 (PRECIS-2) tool allows trialists to consider both pragmatic and explanatory com-ponents across nine domains, shaping the trial design to the purpose intended by the investigators. Aside from the PRECIS-2 tool domains, ED-based investigators conducting PCTs should also consider randomization techniques, human subjects concerns, and integration of trial components within the electronic health record. The authors additionally highlight the advantages, disadvantages, and rationale for the use of four common randomized study design types to be considered in PCTs: parallel, crossover, factorial, and stepped-wedge. With increasing emphasis on the conduct of PCTs, emergency medicine investigators will benefit from a rigorous ap-proach to clinical trial design. 1248 | Ս

## I NTRO D U C TI O N 

Randomized clinical trials are considered the standard design to assess an intervention's effect due to their ability to minimize con-founding and potential selection biases that could influence the outcome of interest. 1 However, prior analyses of clinical trials have shown that the majority are too small in sample size, thereby lacking statistical power, or are prone to other critical issues in design and execution. 2 With explanatory clinical research often conducted in highly controlled patient populations with strict inclusion criteria, results may not be replicated under real-world conditions. 3 To de-velop valid and reliable treatment effect evidence, the number of clinical trials in the emergency department (ED) setting is increasing, particularly with “pragmatic” clinical trials (PCTs) focusing on the in-tervention effect on outcomes in routine clinical practice. The term “pragmatic” was first used by Schwartz and Lellouch 4 to describe approaches to trial design comparing two treatments under the con-ditions in which they would be applied in practice. In general, PCTs are distinguished from explanatory trials by three key attributes: 1) an intent to inform decision makers (e.g., patients, policymakers, cli-nicians) rather than elucidating a biological or social mechanism, 2) an intent to enroll a representative population relevant to the deci-sion in practice, and 3) either an intent to streamline procedures and data collection or measuring a broad range of outcomes. 5 Few clin-ical trials can be fully pragmatic, but efforts to prioritize features of pragmatic trials when feasible should be considered by emergency medicine investigators given the increasing emphasis placed on dis-semination and implementation of interventions with proven benefit in real-world settings. 6–9 As the pendulum continues to swing more toward value-based care, Medicare and other payers, as well as the National Institutes of Health (NIH), have shown an increasing interest in the conduct of PCTs. For example, Medicare and United Healthcare insurance coverage decisions are being influenced by PCTs of older adults re-ceiving acupuncture for low back pain and neutralizing antibodies for COVID-19. 10,11 The NIH Health Care Systems Collaboratory, sup-ported by the NIH Common Fund and multiple institutions, is a par-ticular example of a broader initiative aiming to improve the ways in which PCTs are conducted. To support the design and rapid execu-tion of PCTs across health care systems, the NIH Collaboratory has also developed the electronic Living Textbook including expert con-sensus, standard approaches, best practices, peer-reviewed articles, and guidance documents related to the conduct of PCTs. 12 Despite the increased interest in PCTs, investigators are being increasingly asked to “do more with less." Adjusted for inflation, the average R01-equivalent grant award amount has remained essentially stagnant over the past 25 years. 13 With limited funds available, investigators may encounter challenges meeting desired enrollment numbers, which runs counter to the often-needed greater enrollment within PCTs given their variability and flexibility of intervention develop-ment and assessment. To discover nonneutral results of novel in-terventions and treatments, ED investigators must balance the possibility of it simply being too hard to find a “signal” of treatment difference that overwhelms the “noise” of potential reduced sample size and increased variation inherently present within PCTs. 14 To overcome these challenges and conduct an efficient trial, the planning phase of PCTs is central to its success and requires some-what different approaches to study design, data collection, and eth-ical oversight compared to traditional clinical trials. 15 However, a guide for planning and conducting ED-based PCTs is lacking despite the increasing call for their completion. This article reviews concepts related to ED-based PCTs, including: 1) the PRagmatic Explanatory Continuum Indicator Summary 2 (PRECIS-2) framework, 2) addi-tional key study considerations, and 3) illustrative ED-based exam-ples. The goal of this article is to provide a resource for emergency medicine trialists to reference in the study design phase when plan-ning ED-based PCTs given intervention characteristics and available resources. 

## TH E E X PL A NTO RY– PR AG M ATI C S PEC TRU M 

When establishing the research question to evaluate an inter-vention, investigators must consider the explanatory–pragmatic spectrum. Trials are rarely completely explanatory or completely pragmatic in nature. Frequently, components of both are present, suggesting that a trial may fall somewhere on a continuum based on decisions made by investigators. Explanatory trials are conducted under ideal settings to standardize intervention delivery often with research staff on hand to enroll and administer the intervention it-self. Explanatory trials tend to have fairly restrictive inclusion and exclusion criteria, often resulting in a small proportion of individuals, with comparable clinical and demographic characteristics, at risk for the condition of interest to be enrolled. Explanatory trials answer the question, “Does intervention X work under ideal conditions?” and typically is aligned with clinical efficacy research. Conversely, Department Benchmarking Alliance. PCTs answer the question “Does intervention X work in routine clinical practice?” and is more frequently aligned with clinical effectiveness research. Resultantly, explanatory trials generally exhibit a high degree of in-ternal validity while pragmatic trials prioritize generalizability and external validity. 16 With widespread concern that explanatory trials may be poor predictors of real-world effectiveness, the original PRECIS tool was developed to help investigators work through study design decisions to avoid designing a trial that did not meet their own intentions. 17 In 2015, the PRECIS-2 wheel diagram was developed and offers a framework guide for trialists to consider the pragmatic or explan-atory nature of their trial across nine domains, including eligibility, recruitment, setting, organization, flexibility—delivery, flexibility— adherence, follow-up, primary outcome, and primary analysis. 17,18 Domains are rated from 1 (very explanatory) to 5 (very pragmatic). ED investigators should strongly consider the use of the PRECIS-2 wheel diagram during the study design phase to increase chances that results of the trial are generalizable across the intended practice settings (Figure 1). 

## PR EC I S - 2 CO N S I D E R ATI O N S I N E D - BA S E D P C T D E S I G N 

Unique challenges exist when conducting PCTs in the ED setting that span the PRECIS-2 domains. For trials involving time-sensitive conditions in the ED, one characteristic of note is the brief thera-peutic window for decisions surrounding critical procedures. 14 The PreVent trial is an example ED- based study of bag–mask ventilation during tracheal intubation that addressed pragmatic approaches to time-sensitive conditions by strategically placing randomization envelopes, ensuring broad eligibility criteria, paring down the data collection form to the minimum information required, and having a nonproceduralist that was familiar with the procedure complete the form. 14,19 Second, the broader ED population may also include patients who are not regular visitors to that health system, thereby limiting electronic health record (EHR) data available at the point of care, in comparison to PCTs performed in the primary care or out-patient cardiology settings, as examples. Third, and to be discussed further, is the added complexity surrounding capacity and consent for certain vulnerable ED populations with mental illness or sub-stance use disorder. Researchers face multiple decisions when conducting clinical tri-als, with the planning phase of the trial serving as a critical step to optimize robust and meaningful study findings. Lack of foresight to address potential pitfalls a priori or rushing into study enrollment can leave the investigator searching for ways to “save” the trial post hoc. Detailed below, the nine domains within the PRECIS-2 framework are expanded upon to identify decision points for investigators to consider in the design of ED-based clinical trials. 17,20–24 Each domain is not meant to be a “yes” or “no” in regard to a pragmatic approach, but instead the PRECIS-2 framework is rather a series of decisions to fit a trial design to the purpose intended by the investigators. Eligibility criteria—Enrolling all individuals in a clinical setting with minimal eligibility criteria is a hallmark of PCTs. If an intervention has been previously shown to not be beneficial for children, then a reasonable pragmatic design decision would be to exclude only that population. However, if there remains clinical equipoise regarding an intervention's efficacy across populations of interest, then the most pragmatic approach would be to have very limited exclusion criteria. 2. Follow-up—Compared to usual care, a pragmatic approach to this domain involves trials that have no more follow-up than usual care and do not rely on additional data collection. ED trialists are typically interested in the brief follow-up time period immedi-ately after receipt of the intervention. If follow-up does not differ in care management compared to usual care, then trialists may gather short-term outcomes without undue burden to patients or compromise to the pragmatic nature of the domain. 8. Primary outcome—A general principle of PCTs is that there should be relatively few endpoints, and the ones chosen should be eas-ily measured and salient to stakeholders. If unknown at the time of investigation, outcomes of significance to stakeholders may be determined by gathering qualitative data through interviews or focus groups. Pragmatic measurement of outcomes may also be completed by EHR surveillance, as opposed to the intensive follow-up assessments often done with more explanatory trials. Surrogate outcomes (e.g., process outcomes or other lead met-rics) can be misleading due to potential nonlinear relationships between some surrogate endpoints and the clinical outcome of interest. However, these may be more readily available and thus appropriate for interpreting the impact of identified results. Composite endpoints, combining at least two component out-comes of interest, may be difficult to interpret given the wide variability of clinical importance with regards to individual com-ponent endpoints. 34 Resultantly, the pragmatic nature of a study may be decreased when investigators select surrogate outcomes only important to clinicians (e.g., blood test), use a composite out-come with component parts not important to patients, or meas-ure short-term outcomes when longer term outcomes are more relevant. 35 9. Primary analysis—Using all available data in an intention-to-treat analysis is generally recognized as a more pragmatic approach. Excluding nonadherent participants (per-protocol analysis) or study sites that recruit a lower volume would suggest a more ex-planatory approach to this domain. However, a per-protocol anal-ysis may be considered as a secondary or explanatory analysis for future hypothesis generation. CRASH2 trial is one well-known exam-ple of an ED-based pragmatic trial that started with the end in mind. ## A D D ITI O N A L S T U DY CO N S I D E R ATI O N S FO R P C Ts 

Aside from domains within the PRECIS-2 framework, ED-based in-vestigators must also consider several other decision points during the design phase. While not completely exhaustive, this list includes randomization, human subjects concerns, and EHR integration. 

## Randomization 

Randomization is the process of assigning participants by chance to groups that receive different treatments, without influence by the investigator. Randomization offers two critical benefits, namely, the reduction of selection bias and the avoidance of known and, more importantly, unknown confounders. Bias in clinical trials is described as a systematic error that encourages one result or outcome over another based on methodological errors. While chance imbalance may arise, 37 selection bias includes systematic differences in base-line characteristics between the compared groups and can gener-ally be overcome with adequate randomization techniques and trial sample size. Specific techniques of randomization depend on the random-ization unit, including individual participants or clusters (e.g., entire EDs, health systems) with cluster randomization particularly relevant to PCTs. Individual randomization results in each participant receiv-ing an experimental intervention, a comparator therapy (e.g., usual care), or a placebo when no interaction among trial participants is anticipated after randomization. Cluster randomization involves groups of participants being assigned to the same study conditions in which interaction among participants within the same clustered is anticipated or unavoidable before and after randomization. Key questions for investigators to consider in determining if individual or cluster randomization is appropriate include 38 : Is the phenomenon of interest something that takes place primarily at the level of the individual patient or study participant (e.g., response to an exper-imental drug)? Is the proposed intervention delivered at the level of the group (e.g., adoption of a new treatment guideline)? If ran-domized at the individual level, would it be difficult for clinicians to avoid contamination? Cluster randomized trials are preferred when there is potential for significant treatment contamination—i.e., par-ticipants randomized to the control group may receive aspects of the intervention. Contamination has the potential to reduce the study's reliability and can also decrease the observed differences between groups, therefore biasing results toward the null hypothesis. 39 To be discussed below, two key examples of cluster-randomized trials in-clude parallel and stepped-wedge designs. 40 Of note, clinician-level 1252 | Ս

randomization may be considered in either individual or cluster-randomized techniques depending on the target of the intervention and the objective of the trial. From an analytic perspective, it is important to note that out-comes of participants within a cluster may be correlated. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) is a standard measure of how similar outcomes of individuals within the same cluster are likely to be. 41 With ICC values ranging from 0 to 1, individual out-comes within clusters are increasingly correlated with one another as the ICC increases. Intuitively, if the ICC is zero, then a cluster-randomized trial will often behave just like an individual-level RCT. In the most extreme case when the ICC is 1, a cluster-randomized trial will behave like an RCT with a sample size equal to the num-ber of clusters because the outcomes will simply be identical within each cluster. In practice, the reported ICC values are usually in the 0.05–0.1 range. However, it has been noted that even a small ICC can lead to a substantial sample size inflation relative to an individ-ual level RCT, especially when the cluster size becomes large. 42 If considering cluster randomization, the goal should be to determine the randomization unit that yields the most clusters, while still being feasible to deliver the intervention without risk of contamination. A greater number of clusters provides improved statistical properties when analyzing cluster-level data by increasing power and reducing potential imbalances of baseline characteristics. Additionally, there are several approaches to balance between-cluster differences, including pair matching, stratification, and constrained randomiza-tion. 39,43 Prior to planning the study, emergency investigators should partner with biostatisticians to optimize randomization approaches and determine a preliminary ICC to facilitate accurate sample size estimation. 44 

## Human subjects concerns in PCTs 

Ethical review from institutional review boards (IRBs) is a key com-ponent in the conduct of all clinical research, 45 with the implementa-tion of PCTs often accompanied by unique challenges. 46 With PCTs often recruiting across several institutions, lead investigators typi-cally will use a single, centralized IRB to eliminate redundant reviews of the same material across multiple sites with reliance agreements between local intuitional IRBs and the central IRB. These reliance agreements defer to the centralized IRB's protocol determinations thereby overcoming the need for local amendment determinations across study sites and substantially increasing efficiency of the pro-tection of human subjects review process. 45 To further streamline IRB review, investigators may benefit from convening calls with IRB administrators before the protocol is submitted at each institution to help understand up-front concerns that may delay participant enrollment. Regulatory boards often recommend that any human subject provide written informed consent. However, proponents of PCTs have noted that existing standards for informed consent are in-compatible with a pragmatic study's nature and intent. 47 Waivers of informed consent are becoming increasingly common, with investi-gators required to meet four criteria of the Common Rule (45 Code of Federal Regulations [CFR] 46.116) 48,49 : 1) research must present no greater than minimal risk to subjects, 2) waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects, 3) re-search could not practicably be carried out without the waiver or alteration, and 4) whenever appropriate, the subjects will be pro-vided with additional pertinent information after participation. To be considered by ED investigators, public approval has also been expressed for exception from informed consent (EFIC) in emergency clinical trials. 50 As an ED-based example, Martel et al. 25 used an EFIC to study the treatment of acute agitation given previously described limitations with obtaining informed consent among intoxicated ED patients. 51 In collaboration with the institutional IRB, the authors additionally performed “community consultation,” by reviewing the study protocol with local detoxification facilities, acute psychiatric treatment facilities, and residents of facilities for homeless patients with alcohol use disorder. 25 It is important to note that the third criterion (i.e., waiver or modification of planned consent) is not met by inconvenience, cost, time, speed, or other resource demands to the team of investigators. In the case of ED-based PCTs, “practicality” does not need to refer solely to the ability to conduct the study at all , but also includes if the study's goals are unlikely to be achieved. 52 Counter to the goal of PCTs, nonroutine workflow procedures associated with informed consent process can hinder recruitment, introduce selection bias, and impact generalizability. In determining whether a waiver or modification of planned consent may be appropriate for ED-based PCTs, three questions pertaining to practicality outlined previously by Kalkman et al. 48 should be considered. First, “Is the loss of data quality caused by selection bias or inability to recruit a sufficient number of patients, and can this loss be reasonably attributed to regulatory consent?” Second, “Is the expected loss of data quality so extreme that the trial is not worth doing?” Finally, “Apart from mod-ifying regulatory consent, are there no means or resources available that may be reasonably expected to counter the loss of data qual-ity?” Aside from a waiver of consent, additional options for consent in ED-based PCTs may include broadcast notification, 53 opt-out con-sent, 54 a “short-form” consent, 55 or electronic consent. 56 

## EHR integration 

An additional key study consideration is the role of the EHR in ED-based PCTs. Integration of PCT interventions within existing clinical workflows and data streams is essential to limit the costs and burden of ongoing intervention testing. 57 EHR integration requires early en-gagement with local information technology staff to reach consensus on protocol details and to build the necessary technological infra-structure for the trial. Previous PCT studies have used the EHR for eligibility determination, intervention delivery, and outcome measure-ment, yet prior work has identified challenges. Primarily, these limita-tions have been related to a lack of EHR data interoperability across Ս | 1253 GETTEL ET AL .heterogeneous systems, a lack of usable interfaces and standard workflows, and the inadequate ability to collect clinically appropriate outcome data. 58 Aside from more widespread incentives needed to in-vest in interoperability and the routine collection of patient-reported outcomes, investigators conducting ED-based PCTs would benefit from working with their health care organization to promote EHR standardization (e.g., developing algorithms or computable pheno-types for patient identification) and avoiding overly customized digi-tal interventions at individual sites in multicenter PCTs (Figure 2). 57,59 Phenotyping allows for the identification of patients with concern for particular conditions or potential for improvement after a spe-cific treatment or intervention. Maximizing the phenotyping poten-tial of the EHR may be particularly critical in the time-sensitive ED environment when investigators or clinicians are attempting to over-come treatment response heterogeneity. 14,60

Parallel-group trials in the ED have studied pediatric septic shock treat-ment, 62 computerized clinical decision support to streamline the work-flow for ED-initiated buprenorphine/naloxone and referral, 63 ketamine infusion for acute sickle vaso-occlusive crisis, 64 and shared decision mak-ing in low-risk chest pain. 65 Crossover trial design types overcome the ethical limitations of a placebo control group by allowing all participants to receive the intervention, just in a different order. Of note, an adequate washout period must be included to eliminate the carryover effect from the intervention that was first delivered. 66 Previous crossover trials in the ED have assessed optimal airway management in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, 26 head positioning in acute stroke, 67 and fluid resus-citation in noncritically ill patients. 30 Factorial (2 × 2 or more) design trials allow study of multiple interventions or multilevel interventions in varying combina-tions. Although this design type allows for comparisons between smaller sample sizes, investigators conducting full factorial design studies often need to ensure the trial functions as two indepen-dent RCTs without interaction between the two treatments. 68 In the presence of interaction between two treatments, variations in treatment effect estimands exist and more sophisticated mod-eling techniques should be considered to account for such an in-teraction effect. 69 Factorial designs have rarely been employed in the ED setting to date, 70,71 but studies from other disciplines and settings that could be adapted to the ED setting have as-sessed palliative care educational outreach, 72 peer support and reminiscence therapy for persons living with dementia and their caregivers, 73 and dressing and securement of peripherally in-serted central catheters. 74 Stepped-wedge designs may be considered in multicenter studies, particularly when all participants (or clusters) can begin in the control group. As time passes, participants (or clusters) are randomized to the treatment arm in a sequential fashion, with all participants (or clusters) receiving the intervention within the study period. Illustrative ED-based pragmatic trials using stepped-wedge designs have addressed multidisciplinary primary palliative care, 75,76 treatment strategies for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, 77 and paramedic assessment of low-risk trauma patients to selectively transport without immobilization. 78 Group allocation across the PCT study timeframe for common randomized study design types is de-picted in Figure 3. 

## CO N C LU S I O N S 

There is growing interest in ED-based pragmatic clinical trials for their ability to test interventions in real-world settings and develop evidence that is more widely translatable than traditional explana-tory research. To ensure the collection of meaningful results, emer-gency investigators must consider use of the PRECIS-2 tool as well as additional decisions within the study design phase. This article can serve as a guide to navigate the unique advantages and disad-vantages of various design types to be considered by investigators pursuing pragmatic clinical trials.
