R E S E A R C H L E T T E R Laboratory trends in severe MIS-C 

Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) has been recognized as a rare illness associated with a recent coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infection and consists of a fever, labora-tory evidence of inflammation, and multisystem ( ƾ2) involvement. 1,2 A spectrum of illness has been appreciated, and those with severe MIS-C may exhibit significant cardiac disease, shock, and death. 3Given the wide clinical spectrum, identifying children at risk for severe disease is critical to optimizing care. Those at risk for severe MIS-C have been shown to more likely be non-Hispanic black, obese, male, 13–18 years of age, and have higher peak laboratory markers (troponin, brain natriuretic peptide [BNP], ferritin, C-reactive protein [CRP], interleukin 6 [IL-6]). 4 While studies have attempted to iden-tify laboratory predictors of severe MIS-C, they have not accounted for the patients' day of illness (DOI). 5 It is unclear when each of the laboratory markers rise. The objective of this study is to describe the temporal relationship between serial laboratory markers and symptom onset for severe and non-severe MIS-C. Our overall hy-pothesis was that that DOI biomarker trajectories would differ be-tween groups, with greater overall concentrations in severe versus non-severe cases. We performed a retrospective chart review of all patients with MIS-C treated at a single institution from April 1, 2020, to February 15, 2021. Patients met published Centers for Disease Control (CDC) criteria for MIS-C, and severe MIS-C was defined as cardio-vascular shock (need for vasopressors), cardiac arrhythmia requir-ing intervention, or respiratory failure (need for positive pressure ventilation). DOI was defined as the onset of any symptom related to MIS-C, with the first day defined as day 1. Symptom onset was identified using the emergency department (ED) note and was iden-tified on all patients. If symptom onset was not explicitly mentioned in the ED note, the hospital admission note was used. Patients who met criteria for severe MIS-C at any point during the hospital course were included in analysis. Descriptive data for the overall cohort are presented as medians with inter-quartile range (IQR) or proportions. Laboratory values on the day of ED presentation were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine the relationship between repeated measures of laboratory values (outcome) in those with moderate versus severe MIS-C. Based on model diagnostics and visual inspection of residual plots, all lab values, except albumin, were log transformed. Model outputs for transformed variables are interpreted as the percent-age difference in marginal mean lab value in severe versus moder-ate MIS-C (calculated as one-parameter estimate × 100). Covariates were selected based on review of prior studies as well as biologic and/or clinical plausibility and included DOI, age, race, and DOI-MIS-C category interaction (DOI × MIS-C); a random intercept was included in all models. Biologic sex was considered as a covariate but was non-significant for all models and worsened model fit so was ex-cluded. Model fit was assessed using Bayesian Information Criteria and covariance structure was selected using the null model likeli-hood ratio test. A two-tailed significance level was set at 0.05. Data analysis was performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute). This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Central Michigan University. During the study period, we identified 32 patients with severe and 29 patients with non-severe MIS-C with single ED visits. Those with severe disease were older (7.6 vs. 4.9 years) and more often black (59.4% vs. 42.9%), with roughly half (54%) of patients in both cohorts being female. There was no difference in median days of symptoms at ED presentation (4.0 [IQR 3.0–5.0 days] in severe vs. 5.0 [IQR 2.5–7.0 days] for non-severe, p = 0.46). Criteria for severe MIS-C were met in the ED for 10 patients, with 15 meeting criteria on hospital day 1, 3 on hospital day 2, and 3 on hospital day 3, and 1 on hospital day 6. Median DOI for meeting severe criteria was 6 (IQR 4–6). In the severe group, 31 patients were treated with intravenous gamma globulin (IVIG) and 22 with steroid administration. In non-severe patients, 20 were treated with IVIG and 2 with steroids. The median DOI was similar for IVIG administration in severe (5.0, IQR 4.0–6.0 days) versus moderate (6.0, 3.0–8.0 days) groups, p = 0.29. A total of 24 patients received at least one dose of steroids, with 22 in the severe and 2 in the moderate group. Median DOI for first steroid dose was 6.0 (IQR 3.0–8.0 days) for severe versus 8.0 days for moderate. While not all subjects had biomarkers checked on each hospital day, any patient with at least one measured value of the biomarker of interest was included in the model for that outcome. Description of missing biomarker data is provided in the supplement; there were no missing values for any covariates. On day of ED presentation, patients who developed severe MIS-C had greater median troponin (29 ng/ml, IQR 11–183 vs. 11 ng/ml, IQR 4–45.5, p = 0.027); ferri-tin (311.8 μg/L, IQR 188.3–452.7 vs. 137.9 μg/L, IQR 116.2–246.2, 

p = 0.03); and d-dimer (2.44 ng/ml, IQR 1.38–32.9 vs. 1.38 ng/ml, IQR 0.74–2.32, p = 0.034). For the mixed-effects model analysis, only mean BNP and CRP varied significantly by DOI (DOI × MIS-C) between non-severe and severe MIS-C. For CRP, severe MIS-C patients had greater initial CRP that declined faster than non-severe MIS-C. For BNP, initial levels were greater and subsequently declined in severe MIS-C, whereas Supervising Editor: Dr. Elizabeth Alpern Ս | 1259 STANKOVIC ET AL .non-severe patients had a slow increase (Figure 1). For other labo-ratory parameters, trends by DOI were similar for all patients, but the severe MIS-C group had greater mean troponin (185%, 95% con-fidence interval [CI] 46–456, p = 0.002), ferritin (46%, 95% CI ƴ1.1 to 117, p = 0.05), and d-dimer (116%, 95% CI 46–218, p = 0.0002), whereas albumin was 0.6 g/dl lower (95% CI ƴ0.8 to ƴ0.4, p < 0.001). Patients with severe MIS-C have been shown to have higher peak laboratory markers compared to non-severe MIS-C and severe COVID-19. 4 Our data demonstrate this same trend upon ED presen-tation with a higher median troponin, d-dimer, and ferritin. However, when the laboratory trends of each patient were compared by DOI, only the BNP and CRP showed a significant difference. The severe cohort had an earlier increase in both the BNP and CRP, and then a steady decline over the course of the illness. Patients with non-severe disease presented with a lower BNP early in illness, which slowly rose over time. BNP is secreted by cardiac myocytes in the ventricles in response to wall stretch or mechanical load, and levels typically rise reliably with cardiac dysfunction. 6 Thus, the etiology of the decline in BNP levels in patients with severe cardiac disease is unclear. This could represent the natural history of the disease, recognition of cardiac dysfunction with appropriate treatment (fluid restriction or diuresis), or residual confounding. The influence of treatments, including IVIG and steroids, on biomarker concentra-tions and trajectories remains unclear as we did not adjust for these given our small sample size and the complexities of modeling mul-tiple time-varying treatments and their interaction. Determination of whether this represents natural disease course, confounding due to treatments administered, or other patient-level factors requires further study. Our study is limited by sample size and risks inherent to a ret-rospective study from a single site. We did not adjust for multiple comparisons (of investigated biomarkers) as our goal was to minimize false negatives and crude adjustment methods (e.g., Bonferroni) drastically reduce power. 7 While this can increase the false posi-tive rate, we felt the overall benefit outweighed the potential harms given that these biomarkers are routinely obtained but there remains a paucity of data on temporal laboratory trends in MIS-C. Follow-up studies from larger data sets are needed to confirm our findings. In conclusion, we found that patients with severe MIS-C had higher levels of laboratory markers when compared to non-severe MIS-C, with similar trends across DOIs in both groups for most biomarkers. However, the CRP and BNP levels were significantly greater among patients with severe MIS-C earlier in the disease course. Further investigation may reveal that these two markers may help identify patients at risk for severe MIS-C prior to clinical deterioration.

R E S E A R C H L E T T E R Novel quality assessment methodology in focused cardiac ultrasound 

Cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has become a fundamen-tal component of the evaluation of patients in the emergency de-partment (ED) to diagnose cardiac pathology. 1 Quality assessment (QA) is one of the six required elements of diagnostic POCUS exam-inations per the American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP). 2QA is routinely performed to ensure standard of patient care is met and to assess for competency, particularly at the trainee level. It has recently been described that 82% of EM residency programs report use of QA as an assessment tool. 3 It is imperative to provide a reli-able scoring system to limit inconsistencies in the way we are mea-suring clinical skill as it relates to ultrasound. The current grading scale used for QA that is endorsed by ACEP was developed from a consensus report of emergency ultrasound leaders indicating a need for a systematic method to report and com-municate POCUS findings. 2 The ACEP grading scale is a nonspecific grading classification that applies regardless of the type of study performed. 2 This contrasts with other QA grading systems that have been described in an organ-specific manner. Examples of these sys-tems include focused cardiac ultrasound assessment demonstrated by Kimura et al. 4 and focused gynecological emergency ultrasound exam-ination by Salomon. 5 The goal of this study was to determine whether a similar, organ-specific grading scale would be a more reliable method of assessment with improved interobserver agreement. Furthermore, we sought to determine whether an organ-specific grading scale had more variance in the scores that are chosen and therefore more fo-cused feedback to the sonographers performing the studies. We conducted a prospective analysis of the first 200 cardiac POCUS studies performed in our ED that were submitted for QA into our image database in the year of 2020. Four reviewers, who were either emergency ultrasound fellowship trained or current emer-gency ultrasound fellows with at least 9 months of QA experience, scored each of the studies. Two reviewers used the current ACEP grading scale: 1 = no recognizable structures; 2 = minimally recog-nizable structures but insufficient for diagnosis; 3 = minimal criteria met for diagnosis, recognizable structures but with some technical or other flaws; 4 = minimal criteria met for diagnosis, all structures imaged well; and 5 = minimal criteria met for diagnosis, all structures imaged with excellent image quality. 2 The two other reviewers used a cardiac-specific grading scale as previous described by Kimura et al.: 0 = no image obtained; 1 = only cardiac motion detected; 2 = cham-bers and valves grossly resolved; 3 = endocardium and wall thickness seen but incomplete; and 4 = greater than 90% of endocardium and valve motion seen. 3 The primary outcomes were the level of agree-ment between the reviewers, indicating the reliability of the scoring system, and the variability of the scores given to the studies. This study was approved by the VCU institutional review board. The ACEP score was on a scale of 1–5, while the organ-specific score was on a scale of 0–4. For equal comparison, we added 1 to the organ-specific grading. For the primary outcome, the intraclass cor-relation coefficient (ICC) based on two-way random-effect model with a single rater for each grading scale was computed. Ten thousand bootstrapped ICCs were generated to construct 95% confidence in-tervals (CIs) for both grading systems, and a two-sided one-sample t-test was used to determine if there were differences in the boot-strapped ICCs between the two grading systems. The ICC between reviewers for the ACEP grading scale was 0.54 (95% CI 0.410–0.555) indicating moderate agreement, while the ICC between reviewers using the organ-specific grading scale was 0.75 (95% CI 0.600– 0.769) indicating good agreement. These findings were statistically significant with one-sample t-test p-value of <0.0001. The ACEP grading scale mean ( ±SD) was 3.15 ( ±0.693) versus 4.16 ( ±0.967) for the organ-specific grading system. A 95% CI for the variance ratio was constructed to determine whether there were differences in the variability between the two grading systems. The variance of scores using the organ-specific grading scale was found to be more than 1.95 times greater when compared to the scores using ACEP grading scale. The variance among each group of scores using a 95% CI of the bootstrapped variance ratio (1.49–2.51), the organ-specific grading scale was found to have significantly more variability than the ACEP scoring system. The summary figure for the ACEP and organ-specific grading scale are found in Figure 1. This study is a quantitative prospective analysis comparing the current ACEP recommended QA method to an organ-specific method. We found that there was an increased interobserver agreement between reviewers and increased variability of the scores given to the studies when using the organ-specific method compared to the ACEP method. This is particularly important for trainees; they are often the performers of the ultrasound and, as such, the recipient of the QA reports. More direct feedback may expand their knowl-edge base to be implemented in future studies. For example, the top score on the ACEP grading scale states in a nonspecific manner, “all structures imaged with excellent image quality” versus the cardiac organ-specific grading scale states “greater than 90% of endocar-dium and valve motion seen.” This allows the learner to understand why the top score was given and the structures needed to meet this requirement. The opposite is also true, the organ-specific grading scale presents a detailed response and as such suggests direction for improvement on subsequent studies. The use of a standardized focused scoring system may also improve the quality of the images themselves. Salomon 4 demonstrated that the implementation of an organ specific gynecological emergency ultrasound may improve the quality level of ultrasound examinations performed. Our data highlight the importance of QA methodology that pro-motes objectivity demonstrated by high interobserver agreement. POCUS examinations in the ED continue to rise, and as they do there is a need for a standardized method to perform QA that has been thoroughly validated prior to implementation. This single-center study is limited by the images being obtained and reviewed at an ac-ademic ED by ultrasound-trained faculty limiting the generalizability. This investigation demonstrates an organ-specific quality assur-ance of focused cardiac ultrasound procedures performed in the ED may give the providers performing the studies a wider range of feed-back with increased inter-rater agreement among those doing the re-views. Given these findings, there may be a benefit to moving toward an organ-specific QA scale for POCUS studies obtained in the ED.

## Abstract Objective: The objective was to identify the most important and impactful peer-reviewed global emergency medicine (GEM) articles published in 2021. The top ar-ticles are summarized in brief narratives and accompanied by a comprehensive list of all identified articles that address the topic during the year to serve as a reference for clinicians, researchers, and policy makers. 

Methods: A systematic PubMed search was carried out to identify all GEM articles published in 2021. Title and abstract screening was performed by trained reviewers and editors to identify articles in one of three categories based on predefined criteria: disaster and humanitarian response (DHR), emergency care in resource-limited set-tings (ECRLS), and emergency medicine development (EMD). Included articles were each scored by two reviewers using established rubrics for original (OR) and review Ս | 1265 KIVLEHAN ET AL 

## I NTRO D U C TI O N 

Global emergency medicine (GEM) is a rapidly growing academic sub-specialty of emergency medicine focused on the strengthening of emergency care around the world. 1 This work takes many forms, such as direct patient care in broadly diverse contexts, humanitarian re-sponse, and system development. The maturation of the subspecialty of GEM has been accompanied by an ever-increasing quantity of aca-demic publications of varying quality. The Global Emergency Medicine Literature Review (GEMLR) was created in 2005 to assist clinicians, re-searchers, and policy makers in identifying key current literature most likely to influence the practice of GEM through its annual review. 2–17 The GEMLR Group has grown along with GEM to serve as a mentoring and networking hub for GEM practitioners around the world. 18 The team changes and grows annually, and term-limits force turnover in leadership positions to allow for an increasingly diverse team. In addition to the annual review, the GEMLR group produces an annual systematic review on an understudied topic and maintains a website for data and literature dissemination. 19–22 Since the inception of the annual review, the number of articles screened for inclusion has grown from under one hundred to tens of thousands. To keep up with this growth, structured technical, communications, and planning committees meet twice annually to revisit and revise the approach to identify the top articles each year. This includes defining GEM, to which the GEMLR group takes an inclusive approach leading to frequent modifications to the search strategy. This iterative approach to article identification and scoring rubrics has been used by other groups. 23,24 This scoping review of the GEM literature seeks to provide an objective and accessible list of the top articles published in 2021 along with an interpretation of current GEM publication trends. 

## M E TH O DS 

The GEMLR procedures used in the 2021 review build upon the approach to identifying top articles established in previous year's reviews. Modifications to the strategy occur most years as a result of committee work, which this year included elimination of the gray lit-erature search and minor scoring rubric changes. The GEMLR meth-ods are outlined in detail in the annually updated procedure manual (Data Supplement S1.) The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist was used for this review (Data Supplement S2). The GEMLR team is selected each year through a competitive process after an annual call for applications. Term limits for leadership positions were recently introduced to promote turnover and enhance diversity. This year, the team consisted of 42 people from 10 countries. Team roles included an editor-in-chief; managing editor; assistant man-aging editor; technical editor; six editors; two assistant editors; 24 re-viewers; and six assistant reviewers based in Australia, Brazil, Canada, England, Ethiopia, The Gambia, Ghana, Scotland, South Africa, and the United States (Appendix A). The GEMLR is unfunded and all team members are volunteers. Conflicts of interest can arise when a team member was an author on a publication identified in the search and are managed through a process outlined in the procedure manual. The search, screening, and scoring process occurs in two blocks to facilitate the quantity of work required. The first search covered January 1 to August 31 and the second search covered September 1 to December 31, 2021. The search string was developed with the support of a librarian to optimize efficiency. Minor overlap with ar-ticles published in 2020 and 2022 occurs due to journal publication and indexing variation. The search string is designed to identify ar-ticles in English, Spanish, and French that address emergency care delivery in lower resourced and humanitarian settings. All articles published in African Journal of Emergency Medicine, Bulletin of the World Health Organization, The Lancet , and Prehospital and Disaster Medicine undergo title and abstract screening due to their historic high rate of included articles (hand search). Case reports, commen-taries, editorials, and other similar narrative publications were ex-cluded. The full PubMed search string is in Data Supplement S3. Historically, a small team of reviewers would perform a manual gray literature search of high yield non–peer-reviewed publications and guideline websites. This year the gray literature search was (RE) articles. The top 5% of articles overall and the top 5% of articles from each cat-egory (DHR, ECRLS, EMD, OR, and RE) were included for narrative summary. 

Results: The 2021 search identified 44,839 articles, of which 444 articles screened in for scoring, 25% and 22% increases from 2020, respectively. After removal of dupli-cates, 23 articles were included for narrative summary. ECRLS constituted the largest category ( n = 16, 70%), followed by EMD ( n = 4, 17%) and DHR ( n = 3, 13%). The ma-jority of top articles were OR ( n = 14, 61%) compared to RE ( n = 9, 39%). 

Conclusions: The GEM peer-reviewed literature continued to grow at a fast rate in 2021, reflecting the continued expansion and maturation of this subspecialty of emer-gency medicine. Few high-quality articles focused on DHR and EMD, suggesting a need for further efforts in those fields. Future efforts should focus on improving the diversity of GEM research and equitable representation. 1266 | Ս GLOBAL EMERGENCY MEDICINE LITERATURE REVIEW 2021 discontinued after a review of prior years revealed an extremely low yield of high-impact GEM articles. Articles retrieved in the PubMed search undergo title and abstract screening for relevance to GEM per predefined criteria outlined in the procedures manual. All reviewers perform practice screening and are given feedback to improve consistency. Two team members, a reviewer and an editor, review each title and abstract followed by a third level of review by both the assistant managing and the managing editor. Screened-in articles are categorized as either original research (OR) or a review article (RE). Original research articles are further categorized as quantitative or qualitative or mixed methods for scor-ing purposes. All articles are also classified as one of three potential GEM article categories: disaster and humanitarian response (DHR), emergency care in resource-limited settings (ECRLS), or emergency medicine development (EMD). All screened-in articles each undergo independent full-text review and scoring by two reviewers. Three scoring rubrics are used for each of the three types of ar-ticles: OR quantitative, OR qualitative, and RE. The scoring for each ranges from 1 to 20 points, with scores spread across four subcat-egories: clarity (RE only), ethics (OR only), rigor, importance, and impact. This year, changes were made to the importance category to clarify scoring related to generalizability and affected population. The full templates are available in Data Supplement S4. The top 5% of all scored articles as well as the top 5% of each article category (OR, RE, DHR, ECRLS, and EMD) are narratively summarized. These summaries are a single page in length and follow a templated structure that includes a single-sentence summary; a brief and objective summary of the article's methods and findings; and an interpretation of the strengths, limitations, and importance to GEM. The summaries are prepared by reviewers and edited by editors. They are meant to serve as an accessible brief summary of the top GEM literature for 2021 (Figure 1). 

## R E S U LT S 

The PubMed search retrieved 44,839 articles, which included 1327 from the hand search. A total of 444 articles met the inclusion cri-teria and went on to have a full-text review and scoring (Table 1 and Data Supplement S5). After duplicates were removed, 23 articles were selected for narrative summarization after being identified as a top article by our predefined criteria (Table 2). Of the selected articles, 14 (61%) were OR and nine (39%) were RE. Of the OR arti-cles, 13 (93%) were quantitative and one (7%) was qualitative. Three (13%) were DHR, 16 (70%) were ECRLS, and four (17%) were EMD. Two of the selected top articles were from the hand search journals and two were COVID-19 related. The narrative summaries of each of the 23 top articles are provided in Data Supplement S6. 

## D I S CU S S I O N 

The quantity of GEM research has continued to grow at a fast rate, reflecting the continued growth of the subspecialty. This year's search identified 44,839 articles, a 25% increase from the 35,970 identified in 2020. A total of 444 articles underwent full-text review, a 22% increase from last year's 364. These increases correspond to the 15% increase in articles that underwent a full narrative sum-mary this year. This precipitous growth rate is likely related to the increased recognition of emergency medicine as a specialty around the world, increased funding opportunities for GEM research, and a growing number of journals focusing on global health. 25–28 Last year's search utilized two distinct search strings to separate COVID-19–related articles from all others; however, this year we did not seek to separately identify articles related to the coronavirus pandemic. While last year's search identified a significant quantity of COVID-19 articles in the search (15%) and among screened-in articles (9.6%), none of the identified top articles were COVID-19 related. This was thought to be related to the relatively lower quality of COVID-19–related articles meeting GEMLR inclusion criteria. 29,30 This year, two COVID-19–related articles were among the top arti-cles, which may reflect an improvement in the quality of COVID-19 research in non–high-resourced settings. The GEMLR editorial board consisting of all current and many former editors meets twice yearly to evaluate and improve policies and procedures, supported by three different committees that are assigned tasks to deliberate and evaluate in-between board meet-ings. Changes were implemented for this year's search affecting the search, scoring, and structural domains. No changes were made to search terms; however, COVID-19–specific selectors were removed. Revision of the hand-search journals occurs on a regular basis to both add promising new journals not immediately indexed in PubMed and to remove journals when all relevant articles from the prior 2 years appear in the core PubMed search. However, no changes were made this year. Minor scoring revisions were made to both the importance and impact subsections to better reflect the generalizability and af-fected populations of a study. F I G U R E 1 Flow diagram of articles selected for review Ս | 1267 KIVLEHAN ET AL The parallels between colonization and GEM are increasingly rec-ognized and the GEMLR group has looked inward this year to discuss authorship equity of both included articles and the review itself. 31–33 The GEMLR reviewers, who are listed as contributing authors in Appendix A , are more geographically diverse than the listed authors. GEMLR authorship positions are determined as outlined in the pro-cedures manual (Data Supplement S1), with all authors required to have previously served as a reviewer. Author-level role term limits were tightened this year to accelerate turnover from the increasingly diverse reviewer group. Additionally, GEMLR annual recruitment ef-forts have broadened to advertise via several emergency medicine groups outside of North America in an effort to promote member-ship diversity. A review of the GEMLR's included papers over the past several years has clearly demonstrated authorship inequity between high- and low-and-middle-income countries. 34 Changes to scoring rubrics are planned for next year to address local authorship representation, and future committee work will evaluate the role of funding channels in GEM research equity. The papers reviewed each year by GEMLR are broadly heteroge-nous and not amenable to a formal systematic review or meta-analysis. The scoping review format allows for the annual identification of a diverse set of original research and reviews, and the application of a rigorously developed scoring system provides confidence in article selection. The topics and importance of this year's top articles are briefly discussed below. The full list of scored articles is presented in Data Supplement S5 as a searchable and sortable spreadsheet and the full narrative summaries can be found in Data Supplement S6. 

## Disaster and humanitarian response 

Cavaliere and colleagues 35 reviewed publicly available data from the Global Terrorism Database and identified 901 incidents in 74 countries targeting health care facilities from 1970 to 2018. This work brings attention to this persistent and widespread threat to health care workers and patients around the world. In a system-atic review of the quality of health systems in humanitarian set-tings covering 2010 to 2019, Jordan and colleagues 36 found that a disproportionate emphasis is placed on system foundations rather than competency of care, population health, or economic or societal benefits. Emphasizing the importance of quality of care, they report the common finding that absence of a health care provider led to better outcomes than the presence of a “noncompetent” one. The third and final DHR article included is a systematic review of health system responses to disasters during the COVID-19 pandemic by Sohrabizadeh and colleagues. 37 Their findings demonstrate the chal-lenge of balancing individual and public health while responding to acute events such as earthquakes, floods, and wildfires in addition to highlighting preparedness and response strategies. 

## Emergency care in resource-limited settings 

As in prior years, ECRLS constituted the majority of top articles, many of which were pediatric oriented. In a randomized controlled trial of children with severe pneumonia in Africa, Maitland and col-leagues 38 demonstrated a mortality reduction with high-flow nasal therapy (HFNT) compared to low-flow oxygen and permissive hy-poxemia. While this is the largest multicenter controlled trial of oxygen therapy conducted in a pediatric population, it was termi-nated early due to ethical concerns around withholding oxygen in one arm. Notably, their data showed that HFNT with or without oxygen reduced mortality. Sessions and colleagues 39 evaluated con-tinuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for nonneonatal pediatric respiratory distress in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The authors' findings cast doubt on the efficacy of CPAP for pediatric respiratory distress in LMICs, and further point out that while an oxygen concentrator can only provide CPAP for one child at a time, it could instead deliver low-flow oxygen to five children simultaneously. Al Hussain and colleagues 40 performed a systematic review demonstrating ability of two pneumonia severity scores, CURB-65 and CRB-65, to predict mortality among adults in LMICs. Notably, the CURB-65 tool was superior but the CRB-65 tool was still use-ful in settings where blood chemistry testing is unavailable. As most widely used risk prediction scores have not been validated in LIMCs, this work provides practitioners in LMICs with an evidenced-based tool for triage. In another article focused on severity scoring, Barry and colleagues 41 performed a secondary analysis of data from the Novel, Innovative Research for Understanding Dehydration in Adults and Kids (NIRUDAK) study, which evaluated acute diarrhea manage-ment in Bangladesh, to derive and internally validate a nurse-led 13-point scoring tool to predict the severity of diarrhea in patients over 5 years of age. The discriminatory values of the tool were acceptable and should now be evaluated externally. Ayede and colleagues 42 implemented the World Health Organization (WHO) outpatient treatment guidelines for neonates 0–59 days old with possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI) when inpatient referral is not possible at eight outpatient primary health care centers in southwest Nigeria. Over a 16-month period, trained community resource persons identified 1214 newborns with PSBI of which 91.5% declined hospital referral and were treated at home. All patients with pneumonia were successfully treated at home and 98% of those with clinical severe infection were also cured with home an-tibiotic treatment. This important study demonstrates that novel out-patient treatment guidelines can be successfully implemented within existing health system infrastructure resulting in reduced infant mor-bidity and mortality when social barriers to care are considered and addressed in a contextually relevant and practically applicable man-ner. The use and efficacy of empiric antibiotic therapy for neonatal sepsis in seven countries was evaluated by Thomson and colleagues 43 in an observational study. Although the WHO first-line recommenda-tion of ampicillin and gentamicin was among the most commonly used antibiotics, 379 (97.2%) and 274 (70.3%) of 390 Gram-negative iso-lates were resistant to ampicillin and gentamicin, respectively. These findings suggest the need to revisit the current guidelines in LMICs. In a randomized controlled trial of treatment for pediatric acute nonbloody watery diarrhea in seven countries, Ahmed and colleagues 44 found no survival benefit to the addition of a 3-day course of azithromycin to standard case management. These find-ings add valuable evidence to support adherence to current WHO case management guidelines including zinc, rehydration, and nutri-tional counseling for the treatment of pediatric acute watery diar-rhea in low- and middle-income settings. Focusing on malnutrition in children, a study performed by Charle-Cuéllar and colleagues 45 in Mauritania found that children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) treated by community health workers (CHWs) were found to have similar SAM cure and follow-up failure rates as those treated by tra-ditional outpatient health facilities in a nonrandomized controlled study. This suggests that CHWs can help bridge the gap between access and delivery of treatment for SAM, particularly in resource-limited settings. Road traffic accidents were found to the be the most common cause of pediatric traumatic brain injury (pTBI) in a systematic re-view of the causes of pTBI performed by Bandyopadhyay and col-leagues. 46 Their review covered 32 LMICs and demonstrated that pTBI patients in LMICs are younger than those in high-income coun-tries and more often pedestrians than vehicle occupants. The au-thors also highlighted a gap in pTBI knowledge as data were only available from 26% of 135 LMICs. In an evaluation of trauma sys-tems, Whitaker and colleagues 47 used the three-delays framework, previously used to characterize barriers to maternal health care, to perform a systematic review of the literature on LMIC trauma care systems. Delay 1 considers barriers to seeking care, Delay 2 looks at barriers to reaching care, and Delay 3 concentrates on barriers to receiving care. The authors found that Delay 3 was the most studied, with facility assessments being the most common tool, and concluded that in addition to whole health system injury research, increased research on Delays 1 and 2 are needed. Rabies and meningococcal meningitis remain major public health issues in the world. Salahuddin and colleagues 48 showed that a shortened 1-week rabies postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) schedule was equivalent to the standard 4-week schedule in Pakistan. Despite an increased number of patients requiring PEP during the study pe-riod, there was less use of rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin vials, cost savings, increased patient adherence, and no reported deaths. Rondy and colleagues 49 compared the performance characteristics of two rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) compared with traditional PCR-based tests to detect meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis and 

Streptococcus pneumoniae in Burkina Faso and Niger. They found that the RDTs met WHO acceptable standards, providing evidence to support this diagnostic tool. Risk factors for delays in the diagnosis and treatment of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in LMICs were identified in a systematic review by Beza and colleagues, 50 identifying many targets for future work in this area. Individual risk factors included lower socioeco-nomic status; female gender; older age; and comorbid conditions of diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, while systemic risk factors included rural location, lack of transportation, ambulance availabil-ity, and lack of education surrounding ACS for both patients and clinical staff. Turning attention to the fluid resuscitation of burns, Leclerc and colleagues 51 evaluated the efficiency of simplified for-mulas that could be helpful in mass casualty and disaster scenarios when resources may be scarce. In a mathematical analysis, Leclerc and colleagues compared the WHO Technical Working Group for Burns recommendation of 100 mL/kg over 24 h either orally or intra-venously for burns larger than 20% total body surface area to exist-ing guidelines. They concluded that although it underestimates fluid volumes in small children and in people with large burns, this simpler formula should be appropriate in mass burn casualty situations. In a multicenter randomized controlled trial of the effectiveness of tranexamic acid (TXA) or placebo for patients acute GI bleeding, Roberts and colleagues 52 showed that TXA did not reduce mortality and also that it increased the risk of venous thromboembolic events and seizures. This large study, performed in 15 countries spanning income levels, has produced strong evidence that TXA should not be used in patients with acute GI bleeding. A large randomized con-trolled trial conducted in Brazil on COVID-19 treatment early in the pandemic evaluated two medications against placebo, hydroxychlo-roquine and lopinavir-ritonavir. Reis and colleagues 53 found that nei-ther medication reduced 90-day hospitalization or death, impacting global COVID-19 treatment recommendations. 

## Emergency medicine development 

The first of the four included EMD articles is a systematic review assessing the effects of layperson emergency care training in low-resource areas by Orkin and colleagues. 54 They included 34 papers and concluded that while layperson training for acute interventions is widespread and logical, there is limited evidence for a health ben-efit in this context in the existing literature. Hands and colleagues 55 demonstrated a decrease in pediatric mortality at health care fa-cilities in Sierra Leone after implementation of Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment Plus (ETAT +). The authors used a prag-matic, mentored approach to ETAT + implementation, which is criti-cal to sustained use and impact. This paper adds to the growing body of evidence that improving the process of emergency care leads to improved patient outcomes, including reduced mortality. Ong and colleagues 56 performed a large-scale controlled imple-mentation of dispatcher-assisted bystander CPR for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in the Asia-Pacific region. While they did demonstrate a significantly higher increase in bystander CPR rates and favorable neurologic outcome in the intervention arm, a large majority of data was from high-income counties with less than 10% of recorded OHCA events having occurred in an LMIC, reducing the generalizability of the findings. The final EMD article is a cross-sectional observational study of physician level of agreement on conditions requiring trauma team activation regardless of country income level by Waydhas and colleagues. 57 Through purposive sam-pling and using Delphi methodology, they found that criteria related to abnormal vital signs and need for certain emergency invasive pro-cedures such as airway management had the highest levels of agree-ment across country income levels while acknowledging that some criteria may not be readily available in all settings. 

## LI M ITATI O N S 

There are limitations to the GEMLR's approach to identifying top articles each year. The search terms are reviewed and revised each year to be as inclusive as possible; however, it is possible that some relevant articles are missed due to the broad and heterogenous nature of GEM. Extensive efforts are taken each year to maintain and update objective and complete scoring rubrics to identify top articles; however, some subjectivity in assigning points remains. Each year the GEMLR technical committee revisits these processes based on input from reviewers; details of this can be found in Data Supplement S1. 

## CO N C LU S I O N S 

The continuously expanding quantity and quality of global emer-gency medicine literature is an indicator of the maturation of this subspecialty. The Global Emergency Medicine Literature Review has continued to evolve to keep up with this growth by diversifying its team and improving its search, screening, and scoring procedures. Emergency care in resource-limited settings continues to be the largest area of global emergency medicine research, and the lower quantity of disaster and humanitarian response and emergency medicine development studies suggests a need for increased re-search in those areas. Future Global Emergency Medicine Literature Review work should align with efforts to diversify and decolonize global emergency medicine while serving as a hub for academic mentorship and networking.

## BAC KG RO U N D 

The Society for Academic Emergency Medicine has launched an ini-tiative called GRACE, which stands for Guidelines for Reasonable and Appropriate Care in the Emergency Department. The second iteration of these guidelines examine the issue of low-risk, recur-rent abdominal pain in the emergency department (ED). 1 Abdominal pain is a very common chief complaint in emergency medicine, and its evaluation is relatively resource intensive, with imaging ordered in more than 50% of patients. 2 There is evidence that we overuse imaging in this population, as the rate of CT increased from 10% in 2001 to 22.5% in 2005, while the rate of hospital admission and diagnosis of important pathology such as appendicitis and divertic-ulitis remained unchanged. 3 There is a small population of patients who make frequent visits to the ED for recurrent, undifferentiated abdominal pain. 4 The cumulative risk of ionizing radiation from re-peated CTs increases the risk of harm in this population, but that harm must be weighed against the possibility of a new acute di-agnosis on any given ED visit. 5,6 Patients with repeated visits to the ED for the same complaint may warrant different management plans, as it seems irrational to repeat the same, previously fruit-less investigations and treatments time and again. Emergency clini-cians need evidence-based guidance on the management of these complex patients. With the publication of the GRACE-2 guidelines, Broder et al. 1 attempt to provide us with the best evidence around four key questions in the management of patients with low-risk, re-current abdominal pain in the ED. 

## A RTI C LE S U M M A RY 

This is a guideline developed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment Development and Evaluation) meth-odology. This is a structured framework for guideline development that involves performing systematic reviews of identified ques-tions, assessment of the evidence using specific GRADE criteria, and development of recommendations using a specific “evidence-to-decision” framework. The GRACE-2 writing group consisted of emergency physicians from across the United States and Canada as well as a patient representative and a psychiatrist with specialization in pain management. These guidelines focused on low-risk patients, defined as patients between 18 and 65 years of age, without his-tory of acute trauma, pregnancy, active cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, organ transplantation, immunosuppression, previous bowel obstruction, or severe active psychiatric disease. They were inter-ested in recurrent abdominal pain, defined as two or more ED vis-its for a similar complaint within a 12-month period, but excluding repeat visits within the first 30 days (because those may represent the same acute pathology). The group members identified four pri-ority questions which they put through this guideline development process: DiscussingBroder JS, Oliveira JE, Silva L, et al. Guidelines for Reasonable and Appropriate Care in the Emergency Department 2 (GRACE-2): Low-risk, recurrent abdominal pain in the emergency department. Acad Emerg Med . 2022;29(5):526–560.

> HOT OFF THE PRESS: LOW ҃RISK, RECURRENT ABDOMINAL PAIN IN THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT

1. Should adult ED patients with low-risk, recurrent, and previ-ously undifferentiated abdominal pain receive a repeat CTAP after a negative CTAP within the past 12 months? 2. Should adult ED patients with low-risk, recurrent, and previously undifferentiated abdominal pain with a negative CTAP receive ad-ditional imaging with abdominal ultrasound? 3. Should adult ED patients with low-risk, recurrent, and previously undifferentiated abdominal pain receive screening for depression/ anxiety? 4. Should adult ED patients with low-risk, recurrent, and previously undifferentiated abdominal pain receive nonopioid and/or non-pharmacologic analgesics? 

## Q UA LIT Y A S S E S S M E NT 

This is a well-done guideline that addressed an important topic in emergency medicine. They performed a thorough and well-defined literature search. They employed a rigorous approach evaluating the available literature (in following the GRADE methodology). They explicitly discuss their choice of outcomes and their relative values and discuss both harms and benefits of interventions. They tried to be inclusive of multiple perspectives, including involving a patient advocate on their panel. As with all endeavors in evidence-based medicine, there are lim-itations to consider. These guidelines were designed for application in a setting with advanced imaging, laboratory testing, and specialty referral, and so many not be applicable to all clinicians worldwide. Pediatric patients were also explicitly excluded from this guideline. This group identified four priority questions, but there are many other questions that clinicians might ask when caring for these pa-tients, which this guideline does not address. The involvement of a patient representative provides a valuable perspective, but a sin-gle patient cannot possibly represent the myriad of opinions held by our patients. Most importantly, systematic reviews and resultant guidelines can only be as strong as the underlying literature, and this guideline is ultimately limited by the paucity of research in ED pa-tients with low-risk, recurrent abdominal pain. 

## K E Y R E S U LT S 

The guideline panel identified four key questions of interest, and after a systematic review of the literature and evidence synthesis, they make four recommendations. 

Recommendation 1: In adult ED patients with low-risk, recur-rent, undifferentiated abdominal pain and prior negative CT of the abdomen and pelvis within 12 months, there is insufficient evidence to accurately identify populations in whom repeat imaging can be safely avoided or routinely recommended in the ED. (No recommen-dation) [No evidence] 

Recommendation 2: In adult ED patients with low-risk, recur-rent, undifferentiated abdominal pain and a negative CTAP with IV contrast in the ED, we suggest against ultrasound unless there is concern for pelvic or biliary pathology. (Conditional recommenda-tion, against) [Very low certainty of evidence] 

Recommendation 3: In adult ED patients with low-risk, recur-rent, undifferentiated abdominal pain, we suggest screening for depression and/or anxiety may be performed during the ED evalu-ation. (Conditional recommendation, either) [Very low certainty of evidence] 

Recommendation 4: In adult ED patients with low-risk, recurrent, undifferentiated abdominal pain, we suggest an opioid-minimizing strategy for pain control. (Conditional recommendation) [Consensus, no evidence] 

## AU TH O R ' S CO M M E NT S 

The paucity of evidence for such a common and complex problem in emergency medicine is somewhat disappointing. Given the tremen-dous uncertainty that remains about the ideal management plans for these patients, it is essential to involve our patients in shared deci-sion making, and ensure that the chosen management plan aligns with their individual values. 

## TO P SO CI A L M E D I A CO M M E NTA RY 

There was some excellent discussion of these guidelines on the SGEM blog. Among other concerns, Sara says, “I understand the value of a ‘mental health’ history but I feel it minimises and deval-ues these women's symptoms that may very well be physical and that depression/anxiety may be a response to genuine ongoing pain.” Joshua Broder, the lead author of these guidelines, responds, “The GRACE-2 Writing Group shared your concerns about potential stigma of mental health screening or dismissing undiagnosed causes of pain such as endometriosis, and this is discussed in the full guide-line document. The patient representative on the panel provided in-sights as well, and we did our best to balance the potential benefits of identifying a concurrent (though not necessarily causal) relation-ship between depression, anxiety, and pain.” He adds that this issue is addressed in the patient informa-tion document: “I'M HERE FOR ABDOMINAL PAIN. WHY IS THE DOCTOR ASKING ABOUT DEPRESSION? Depression affects as many as 25% (one in four) of people visiting EDs for abdominal pain. Sometimes mental health conditions such as depression cause phys-ical symptoms such as abdominal pain. Sometimes having a long-term painful condition such as abdominal pain can lead to or make depression worse. When your doctor asks about depression, they aren' t saying that your abdominal pain is ‘just in your head.’ They are hoping to find ways to help you feel better. Your doctor knows that you could have a serious cause of abdominal pain, whether or not you have symptoms of depression.” Dan Eickmeier raises some of the problems we face when trying to care for these patients. “When we are losing beds to patient boarding Ս | 1277 HOT OFF THE PRESS in the ER and decreased nursing staffing, can we really be going down the rabbit hole of repeat investigation for what is most likely (especially after one round of comprehensive negative investigations) functional abdominal pain/IBS. I'd love to have a dietician give some counsel on fiber, etc., to all the abdo pain patients we see (also good in diverticuli-tis, hemorrhoids, fissures, etc) but that ain't happening anytime soon.” To which Joshua Broder responds, “I'm excited to see this response, which really poses hypotheses for future research: is some or all recur-rent undifferentiated abdominal pain functional pain/irritable bowel syndrome? Would dietary changes be an effective treatment for some patients? We need more studies to understand the potentially diverse causes of recurrent undifferentiated abdominal pain.” The conversation on Twitter seemed to focus on problems of overinvestigation, and frustration at the lack of available science to guide us: 

Josh Davis (@MedFactChecks): We really need a way to reduce imaging. we all know 20 CT per year is unnecessary, but no one wants to be the last one to miss something. Care Plans really help with this. Even Harder when they have diagnosis of organic (often IBD) disease even though no records to support it. 

Ryan Radecki, MD MS (@emlitofnote): These summaries are just softballs to aspiring early career investigators – “here's a huge im-portant problem, here are the massive holes in the evidence”. Great opportunities to do some retrospective work and build to small grants or Ks. 

Josh Davis (@MedFactChecks): So true. Lots of work and no good science— but lots of opportunities! 

## TA K E-TO - WO R K P O I NT S 

Given the lack of evidence available to guide us, there is tremendous uncertainty in the most appropriate management plan for these patients. We should be open about that uncertainty with our pa-tients and involve them in shared decision-making to ensure that the chosen management plan matches their personal values. Although the current lack of evidence is somewhat disappointing, uncertainty is a core skill of emergency physicians.

There is only so much stress a bridge can take before it fails. Rarely does the stress come in the form of a single catastrophic event—a force so great that the steel twists, bends, and finally crum-bles. Rather, it is more likely that the stress comes in small incre-ments—no one individual load greater than the bridge's ability to withstand it. But over time these repetitive injuries silently and in-sidiously weaken the bridge, until one day—a day that seems like any other—the bridge comes down. Structural engineers have a name for these silent injuries— fatigue. Bridge fatigue is a progressive process in which structural damage accumulates due to the repetitive application of external loadings such as the burden of too many or too heavy vehicles. These applied loadings may each individually be well below the structural resistance capacity—such that a conventional structural stress analysis might lead to an erroneous conclusion of safety on any given day. Yet, the burden over time is unsustainable. This is because the calculus of risk of damage requires a consideration of stress over time, not just a one-time assessment related to a singular event. It 's much more difficult to define structural fatigue when it comes to the practice of medicine—though this is the state we are in with the current mental and behavioral health crisis, with children and adolescents waiting days and weeks in emergency departments (EDs) to receive definitive psychiatric care. Despite the lack of con-crete definitions, the concept of structural fatigue applies—the daily forces that slowly weaken the system to the point that it can no lon-ger serve the purpose for which it was designed. Our providers, our structures, and our system cannot survive these forces much longer, and without intervention, they may crumble. Historically, in medicine, we have focused on singular events as the source of structural fatigue—a provider suffering from “burnout” or a “difficult” patient. Implicit in the concept of burnout is an indi-vidual design flaw, an intrinsic weakness—a bridge not built to with-stand the known strain accompanying its functional load, a human whose resilience is inadequate. Similarly, the “difficult” patient can be written off as a fluke or an aberration—an individual truck whose load was accidentally too heavy for the bridge. This focus on singular events distracts from the systemic analysis that is needed to stabi-lize our structures. The science of bridge fatigue suggests that we need to ask different questions about the load being imposed on our EDs. ED visits among children and adolescents with mental and behavioral health complaints are up over 250% over the past decade, with roughly half of those patients boarding in the ED while waiting on definitive placement. 1,2 Recently, in our 52 bed ED, our providers cared for 39 patients with behavioral health complaints over 24 h, 12 of whom were admitted or discharged and 27 of whom were forced to remain in our ED awaiting inpatient psychiatric place-ment. The adverse patient care outcomes that follow such an in-flux of long-stay behavioral health patients is well known: long wait times for medical and behavioral health patients to be evaluated (8 h +), delayed care for high-acuity patients, increased rates of left without being seen. On this particular day, despite the adverse pa-tient care outcomes and the high provider load, the waiting room was empty by the morning, for some a sign that the bridge had held. But the bridge is silently, inexorably failing. Our EDs are not designed to house large numbers of behavioral health patients for days at a time. The load is too great and the burden over time is unsustainable—and the cracks in the system are beginning to show. Our patients are not getting the care they need and our providers are strained with the moral injury of providing inadequate care. We can wait for the day when disaster strikes—a preventable code in the waiting room, a mass exodus of nurses—or we can apply some of the basics of bioengineering to understand how the chronic load weakens the system and apply mitigation strategies to prevent the inevitable disaster. There is only so much stress a bridge can take before it fails.

C O R R E S P O N D E N C E  ҃ U N S O L I C I T E D L E T T E R S T O T H E E D I T O R How to treat venous aneurysm in emergency department? 

To the Editor: Venous aneurysms are extremely rare. At present, approxi-mately 500 cases have been reported in the literature, and the first symptom is often deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embo-lism, 1 so they have become a very special disease in the emergency department (ED). Venous aneurysms can occur at any age, with the same sex distribution, and can occur in any vein, but they are most common in popliteal vein (45%), portal vein (30%), and supe-rior mesenteric vein (10%). In the process of screening the etiology of venous thromboembolism (VTE), venous aneurysms of the lower limbs is one of the reasons, and popliteal venous aneurysms are the most common. Cystic vein aneurysm is also considered as a high-risk factor for DVT. Surprisingly, anticoagulation alone does not seem to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events (VTE), because venous aneurysms provide an environment for the formation and spread of thrombosis. 2 At least 60% of portal or superior mesenteric vein an-eurysms are at risk of complications, including portal hypertension, rupture and fistulation, and subsequent gastrointestinal bleeding. 3For symptomatic patients or patients with venous aneurysms with signs of thromboembolism, surgical repair is recommended. There is no consensus on the management of asymptomatic pa-tients. The low incidence rate of venous aneurysms makes it difficult to assess the outcome of interventional therapy, long-term treat-ment, and the incidence of postthrombotic sequelae. At present, the management of different centers is not unified, and multiagency cooperation should be encouraged. However, since most patients appear in the ED with their first symptoms, multidisciplinary cooper-ation to treat this disease in the ED should be promoted. Surgery is the main treatment for venous aneurysms. Endovascular treatment of venous aneurysms has not been deter-mined, although endovascular intervention may be suitable for an-atomically challenging venous aneurysms. Cystic venous aneurysms are usually treated by resection of venous aneurysms and repair of lateral veins. Fusiform vein aneurysms can be treated by the follow-ing methods: resection and end-to-end anastomosis, intermediate transplantation and bypass, and proximal and distal venous ligation. 4Superficial venous aneurysms can be treated by venous ligation. Surgical risks include hematoma, wound infection, thrombophlebitis, nerve injury, and recurrence. Individuals usually remain anticoagu-lant for 3–6 months after surgery. The patency rate was estimated to be between 40% and 93%, and venous aneurysm resection and lateral vein repair were associated with the best long-term patency rate. 5 The emergency intervention decision of venous aneurysm is based on the risk balance, considering the risk of rupture and the in-cidence rate of VTE related to the intervention. Although it may not be possible to conduct a standard randomized controlled trial in the ED, it emphasizes the need to register data and combine multicenter retrospective studies to help determine individualized treatment. Is there anything we can still do? ”Yes doctor, although it 's probably not so important for you. Please change the batteries to that damned old clock!

R E F L E C T I O N Just another day Richard J. Cunningham MD 

> Department of Emergency Medicine, Emergency Medicine Resident, PGY-3, Maricopa Medical Center, Phoenix, Arizona, USA

The day starts like any other. I roll in at 6 AM to take sign-out from the overnight team who sport purple bags under their eyes. The board is fairly clean. Nobody is too sick, mostly stable abdominal and chest pain work-ups and a few psych holds pending placement. “Follow up on bed 16s scan, repeat a CK on 20 once he gets his fluids, I'll page surgery after sign-out and circle back, etc., etc.” Just another day. The morning is calm, I sip coffee at my desk when I'm not roam-ing from room to room, pushing on bellies, palpating pulses, probing wounds…. Soon, I get a call on my phone: “EMS is bringing in a full code in 5.” I head up to the resus bay. Just another day , I think to myself. The medics arrive and give report: 24-year-old at a detox facility, witnessed seizure-like activity and emesis, then went unre-sponsive. Received bystander CPR. PEA and asystole at each pulse check, three rounds of epi prior to arrival. Our team goes to work. Pulse check: PEA, back on the chest. Another epi please, bicarb, calcium. Pulse check: PEA, back on the chest. ET tube in place, positive end-tidal. No pneumo on ultra-sound. Pulse check: asystole, back on the chest. Another round of epi. No pericardial effusion. End tidal is dropping. After rounds and rounds of compressions, my H's and T's fail me. “Does anyone have any other ideas?” I announce to the room. I receive silence in return. Pulse check: “Time of death: 9:15 AM.” Just another day , I tell myself. “Let 's have a moment of silence…” Her mother shows up later that morning. I deliver the news. She looks back at me stone-faced. “I was expecting this,” she says. The patient had a long history of mental health and substance abuse problems, not uncommon at our safety-net hospital. It 's only toward the end of our conversation when she shows any emotion, chok-ing back tears “At least I can tell her children that their mother was good and that she went to heaven.” Just another day , I think to myself. Dejected, I leave as the social worker directs her to the morgue. I pick up the next chart: Ear pain. I scrape out a large ball of ceru-men and try to recall the Spanish word for earwax. “Ahhh,” she sighs in relief, “Muchas gracias, muy amable.” From there on, my shift is smooth sailing. I reassure a “GI bleed” that their hemorrhoids are nothing to fret over. I win a wager on a D-Dimer and send the patient home, both of us in good spirits. Hopping over to fast track, I clinch the diagnosis of mallet finger, splint in extension, and move along. 

Just another day , I think, cheering myself on. Some days it 's the little victories that outweigh the big defeats. “The nurse will bring you your paperwork, then you're good to go.” Not the first time I've said it, and certainly not the last. “And don' t forget to make an appointment with your primary doc!” I add as I close the curtain behind me. I head back to my computer, hit the discharge button, and check the clock. 2:02 PM, I've crossed the fin-ish line, no more patients this shift. As the evening shift crew trickles in I update my patients on their results, catch up on notes, and clean up my dispos for sign-out. 

Just another day , I think to myself. Except today is different. After 3 years in the trenches, today is my last shift at the county emer-gency department, my home base. Of course there are 2 months of residency left, but I'll be off-service, working at outside community hospitals, one more month in the MICU and another in the ED. I hand over my patients. I have not told my colleagues, my friends, that today is my last. Given the timing they do not realize it, and it just does not feel right to tell them. Why make a fuss? It really is just another day , I convince myself. I hand in my phone in exchange for car keys and walk out the am-bulance doors into the bright afternoon sun. I look back and contem-plate the hospital and the people inside it who helped form me into the physician I am. I've worked hundreds of shifts and taken care of thousands of patients, but in this job there's always another patient, always another shift, always another turnover. The cycle goes on. Today, like every other day, was just another day .
